detail: Auth redirects on the hunting environment may pass ?next= / ?returnUrl= / ?redirect= parameters through a 'You are being redirected to <url>' intermediate page that reflects the parameter value unencoded. To test: request login/logout endpoints with a canary redirect parameter and inspect the intermediate response for unencoded reflection.
evidence: Untested; SSO/LDAP redirect chains (Q5) typically include redirect parameters; SSO pages are a known reflected-XSS location in enterprise apps.
falsifier: No intermediate page exists (302 redirect issued directly, parameter never rendered), or parameter is reflected only inside href with proper URL validation/encoding.

title: Filename stored XSS in shared-folder listing rendered to collaborators
detail: Kiteworks is a file-sharing/collaboration platform where a shared folder's file list is rendered to OTHER users (collaborators/recipients). Hypothesis: the upload API stores an attacker-controlled filename without sanitization and the folder-listing view interpolates the filename into innerHTML (or an equivalent unescaped sink). Test input would be a filename containing a markup-breaking token (e.g. quote + event-handler token). Confirming behavior: a second user opening the shared folder sees script execution (or any injected markup) in their browser. Because program bounty requires real impact and a CSP header is present, confirming behavior must ALSO survive the CSP (inline execution blocked otherwise).
evidence: No target-specific evidence yet (passive-only phase; upload/login flows not yet mapped). Pattern grounded in collaboration apps generally: filenames are the #1 stored-XSS vector in shared file listings. World model confirms CSP header present, which constrains execution but does not falsify HTML injection.
falsifier: Inspect the shared-folder listing markup (a collaborator view, under ResearchSession + authorization) and the CSP header: if the filename is HTML-escaped in the rendered markup (view-source shows </> entities) OR CSP blocks inline scripts AND no HTML injection lands at all, the hypothesis is rejected. Also rejected if this environment has no sharing/collaborator view that renders filenames.

title: File/folder comment or description stored XSS rendered to collaborators
detail: Collaboration file platforms frequently let users attach comments, notes, or descriptions to shared files/folders, rendered in the victim recipient's file view. Hypothesis: a comment/description field on a shared file accepts HTML (or accepts text that is rendered without escaping) and is displayed verbatim in another user's session. Test input would be a comment containing a safe markup token (e.g. a <b> or quote-token probe) submitted from account A on a file shared with account B. Confirming behavior: the token renders as live markup in B's file view (and, for full confirmation, script executes under the CSP).
evidence: No target-specific evidence yet; comment/description feature existence on this environment is an open question (world-model Q3/Q5). Pattern is classical for file-sharing apps.
falsifier: If the environment has no comment/description/annotation feature on shared files, the hypothesis is rejected outright. If comments exist but render as plain text with entities escaped (verified in B's DOM), rejected.

title: Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms field-label stored XSS rendered to form recipients or admins
detail: Kiteworks 'Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms' is listed as an in-scope product. Forms products render attacker-authored content (field labels, help text, confirmation messages) to other users (form fillers, reviewing admins). Hypothesis: a form creator can author a field label/description containing markup that is stored and rendered unescaped in the filler's or reviewer admin's browser. Test input would be a form field label with a markup token created in a test form. Confirming behavior: the recipient/admin view renders the token as live markup/script.
evidence: No target-specific evidence yet; forms feature is in scope per YesWeHack program description (Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms). Cross-user rendering is inherent to forms workflows.
falsifier: If the hunting environment has no forms feature enabled, rejected. If labels are escaped in the rendered form, rejected. Self-XSS exclusion note: must affect a DISTINCT user (filler/admin), not the form creator's own preview — a creator-only preview rendering is excluded.

title: Attacker-controlled display name / share-invite message rendered to recipient in share UI or HTML email notification
detail: When user A shares a file/folder with user B, Kiteworks renders A's identity (display name, company) and/or a custom invite message in B's share dialog, activity feed, or notification email. Hypothesis: the inviter-controlled display name or invite message is interpolated without escaping into the recipient's share-notification UI (or an HTML notification email rendered in the mail client). Test input would be a profile display name or invite message containing a markup token, then inviting the second test account. Confirming behavior: recipient's share UI or notification shows live markup/script. Note: email-client XSS is environment-dependent; the share-dashboard rendering is the primary target.
evidence: No target-specific evidence yet. Cross-user identity rendering in sharing dialogs is a standard stored-XSS location across file-sharing products.
falsifier: If display names and invite messages are HTML-escaped in the recipient's share UI (verified in rendered DOM), rejected. Rejected for the self-XSS variant (creator's own settings page) — only the RECIPIENT view counts per program rules. Program-excluded: this must not be framed as user enumeration — the test uses two consenting test accounts, not discovery of other users.

title: Login username flows unsanitized into LDAP login filter, changing filter semantics
detail: Kiteworks authenticates directory users by interpolating the submitted login username into an LDAP search filter (docs: login username matched against directory attributes like uid/sAMAccountName/mail per the deployment checklist and ownCloud-family LDAP login-filter design). Hypothesis: metacharacters in the username field (*, ), (, \) are not escaped, so inputs like '*)(uid=*))(&(uid=*' alter the filter's boolean semantics instead of being treated as a literal string. Impact class would be LDAP injection (program-explicitly in scope), not mere enumeration.
evidence: obs_app/obs_diff agents: 'login username matched against directory attributes (uid/sAMAccountName/mail pattern per deployment checklist + ownCloud-family LDAP login-filter design)' and 'LDAP filter-construction points from docs: (1) login username matched against directory attributes'.
falsifier: Submit a metachar username and a benign invalid username of equal length over multiple trials and observe identical response class (same error text, same status code, latency within jitter) — no wildcard effect, no LDAP-error surfacing. OR: the hunting env uses local accounts only (documented in-world-model open question #2), in which case the input never reaches an LDAP filter. NOTE: mere account-existence oracle is user enumeration (program-excluded) and must not be claimed as a finding; only a semantics-changing filter effect counts.
tests: Manual, operator-led: single metachar probes such as '*)(uid=*))(&(uid=*' in the username field vs plain 'no_such_user_zz', comparing error text/status/latency across trials. No automated fuzzing, no password guessing (brute force forbidden), no login attempt beyond the single careful probe authorized under the ResearchSession workflow.

title: /rest/ldapGroups group-name search concatenates into LDAP filter unsanitized
detail: Admin docs describe a REST API for LDAP groups (documented at /rest/index.html) with endpoints including /ldapGroups that expose LDAP groups to end users for folder sharing. Hypothesis: the group-name search parameter is interpolated into an LDAP filter without escaping, so metacharacter input ('*', ')(cn=*)') expands the result set beyond the literal substring match. A wildcard-injected group listing that discloses directory groups not matching the typed string would be an LDAP-injection impact (directory information disclosure via filter manipulation).
evidence: obs_app: 'LDAP Groups section: List LDAP groups (documented at /rest/index.html). Deployment checklist references LDAP groups' and '/ldapGroups/endpoints' exposing LDAP groups to end users; 'LDAP groups can be exposed to end users ... when sharing folders... using /ldapGroups/endpoints'.
falsifier: Request the endpoint (if exposed in the hunting env; anonymous access is not assumed) with a metachar group-name and a plain group-name: result sets identical, i.e. '*' returns exactly the same listing as the literal string, and no LDAP error text surfaces. OR: the endpoint is admin-only/absent in the hunting environment, so the input flow is unreachable.

title: Share-dialog recipient autocomplete directory search is filter-injectable
detail: Sharing flows target LDAP users/groups; the share dialog autocomplete almost certainly performs a live directory search with the typed string as the filter term. Hypothesis: the autocomplete input is concatenated into the LDAP search filter, so a metacharacter string changes which entries are returned (e.g. ')' or '*' widening results or producing an LDAP syntax error). This would be end-user-reachable LDAP filter manipulation, distinct from the admin /ldapGroups endpoint.
evidence: obs_app: 'LDAP groups to be available to end users when sharing folders' and 'Sharing can target users / LDAP groups'; world model: Kiteworks Core file-share flows with permission modeling are open research.
falsifier: Autocomplete results with metachar input are identical to results for the escaped/literal equivalent; typing '*)(uid=*)' returns only entries literally matching that string (or nothing), with no error differential vs an arbitrary no-match string. OR: the share search in the hunting env only searches local/provisioned users, not the directory.

title: Secure-email recipient validation lookup is LDAP filter-injectable
detail: Kiteworks Email Protection Gateway supports 'recipient validation': verifying a recipient is on the original recipient list of an email before allowing a download, backed by LDAP directory lookup (Accellion can verify if a user is on the original recipient list). Hypothesis: the recipient identifier (email/local part) supplied in the validation request is interpolated into the LDAP query filter unsanitized, so metacharacters alter the lookup semantics — e.g. causing a validation pass for a recipient who should fail, or surfacing LDAP errors. A bypass would be a real authorization impact; an error differential alone is not enough.
evidence: obs_app: 'RECIPIENT VALIDATION: Accellion can verify if a user is on the original recipient list of the email for downloading a file. This prevents forwarding links. This is a System Administrators configurable option.'
falsifier: Validation outcome for a metachar recipient is identical to a benign non-matching recipient (both rejected the same way), with no LDAP error text or timing differential; the pass/fail decision never flips on metachar input. OR: recipient validation is disabled/absent in the hunting environment, or the lookup is by exact attribute match server-side before filtering.

title: MFT 'import from URL' / file-request feature performs server-side fetch of attacker-supplied URL
detail: Managed File Transfer products commonly expose an 'import file from URL' or 'download from URL' flow so users can pull remote content into the transfer. If the hunting environment exposes such a flow (e.g., MFT upload dialog with a URL tab, or API endpoint accepting a sourceUrl), the server will fetch the attacker-influenced URL with its own network access.
evidence: MFT is in scope; target is an enterprise file-transfer app where URL-import is a standard convenience feature. No direct evidence yet - feature existence unverified.
falsifier: Enumerate the MFT upload/share UI and API surface (<=10 spaced requests, UA '-public-yeswehack'); if no URL-import/download-from-URL flow exists anywhere, this sink does not exist.

title: Email Protection Gateway fetches remote content from inbound email (URLs/attachments) server-side
detail: The Email Protection Gateway in scope inspects inbound mail; many secure-email gateways fetch remote URLs for reputation/preview (link sandboxing), fetch attachments from URLs embedded in email, or expand shortened URLs. If the hunting environment accepts inbound test email, an attacker-influenced message containing a URL may trigger the gateway to issue a server-side outbound request.
evidence: EPG is explicitly in scope; URL-fetching for phishing/sandbox analysis is standard in email-gateway products. Existence of inbound email acceptance in the hunting env unverified.
falsifier: Confirm whether the hunting environment offers an EPG email-receiving address or mail-flow test path; if no inbound mail path exists in the test env, the sink is unreachable.

title: Link preview / rich-link unfurling in Core file sharing or Advanced Forms fetches attacker-supplied URLs
detail: Kiteworks Core (file sharing/comments) and Advanced Forms (external-facing forms) may generate link previews or unfurl URLs pasted into file descriptions, comments, or form rich-text fields. If so, the server performs a fetch of the user-supplied URL to render the preview.
evidence: Core and Advanced Forms are in scope and are collaboration products where link-preview features are common. Preview endpoint existence unverified.
falsifier: Inspect sharing/comment/form flows; if no link-preview/unfurling behavior is observed in UI or network metadata, the sink does not exist.

title: Webhook/notification configuration or document-conversion fetches attacker-supplied URLs server-side
detail: Two classic secondary sinks: (1) admin-configured webhook/notification endpoints for transfer or form events - if the web UI lets a low-privileged user register a webhook URL, delivery attempts produce server-side requests to attacker-controlled hosts; (2) document/PDF conversion or thumbnail generation of uploaded files that embed remote references (e.g., HTML/DOCX import referencing an external URL). If either exists, attacker-influenced URLs reach server-side HTTP clients.
evidence: API Playground and Advanced Forms imply event/notification and document-processing surface; both are classic SSRF sinks in enterprise apps. Existence unverified.
falsifier: Check integrations/notification settings and document-conversion behavior; if no user-influenced webhook URL registration and no remote-reference fetching during conversion exists, reject.

title: H1: Version-overwrite IDOR via numeric file_id on initiateUpload
detail: Reference pattern: file IDs are small sequential numerics (documented API feedback shows id: 1240), and the new file's ID is returned in the X-Accellion-Location response header after POST /rest/folders/{id}/actions/file. Same-name re-upload creates a NEW VERSION of the existing file rather than rejecting. The new-version path is POST /rest/files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload, which takes a file_id belonging to an existing object. Hypothesis: the initiateUpload-version endpoint checks that the caller has folder membership (or any folder role, e.g. Downloader/Uploader/Viewer) but does NOT verify the caller holds an edit-granting role (Collaborator/Manager/Owner) on that specific file, so a lower-role folder member can force a new version onto a file they cannot edit. Confirming behavior: with two consenting test accounts where account B holds Downloader/Viewer (no edit) on a folder and account A holds a file there, B calls POST /rest/files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload with A's file_id and a lastChunk block, and the server accepts it — a new version of A's file appears attributable to B. This is a targeted variant of the documented upload/authorization seam (CVE-2026-23514-class: authenticated user reaching unauthorized content; CVE-2026-23636-class: upload validation gaps), not the CVE itself (env is 9.5.1).
evidence: obs_app n=22: 'the id specified in the X-Accellion-Location field'; 'POST /files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload (new version)'; 'with the file name already exists in this folder, a new version of this file will be created'; API feedback example shows numeric id: 1240. obs_app n=18/n=19: role ladder Viewer/Uploader/Downloader vs Collaborator/Manager/Owner.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) the endpoint returns 403 for a Downloader/Viewer caller on another user's file_id while the same call succeeds for a Collaborator/Manager (i.e., a per-object role check exists); or (b) file_ids in the hunting environment are non-sequential UUIDs or otherwise unguessable so B cannot address A's file without out-of-band knowledge — though even then the check must still hold for shared/granted files; or (c) the endpoint scopes entirely by folder and documents that any folder member may version any file (a designed semantic, not a bug).

title: H2: Viewer-role download bypass via direct REST content fetch
detail: Reference pattern: numeric file IDs (id: 1240 class) exposed through search results — docs confirm search results carry creator/userId metadata per item and there is NO server-side owner filter, so a Viewer learns file IDs of objects beyond their intended capability. The Viewer role is defined as view-only through the Online Viewer with NO download permission. Hypothesis: the direct content endpoint (GET /rest/files/{file_id}/content or equivalent byte-serving endpoint) checks authentication and folder membership but not the Viewer-vs-Downloader role split, so a Viewer can pull raw file bytes they are only allowed to render in-browser. Confirming behavior: a test account holding only Viewer on a shared folder issues the direct content GET for a file_id learned from its own search result and receives 200 with the file bytes, while the web UI offers it only the render view. NOTE: this is a folder-role check bypass, NOT 'anyone after authentication' disclosure (program-excluded class) — the caller is an intended recipient of the share but with a denied capability.
evidence: obs_app n=33: 'Online Viewer: Viewers can view documents within the browser or Mobile App without being granted permission to download them'; obs_diff n=26: 'there is NO server-side owner or creator filter on search'; 'Every search result carries creator/userId metadata visible to the searcher'. obs_app n=25 handoff flagged 'whether role checks (Viewer cannot download) hold on direct /rest/files/{id}/content access' as a testable seam.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) the direct content endpoint returns 403/denied for a Viewer caller on the same file the UI renders for them (role check present on the byte path, not just the UI); or (b) the content endpoint re-checks capability via a distinct authorization call and degrades to Online Viewer render only; or (c) the hunting environment does not expose a direct byte endpoint to non-Downloader roles at all.

title: H3: Folder activity-log / mail Track report readable by non-privileged identity via ID swap
detail: Reference pattern: numeric folder/mail object IDs (same sequential ID space as files, e.g. id: 1240) used in the REST paths /rest/folders/{id}/members and the web-app Details tab and sent-mail Track report endpoints. The folder Details/activity log (timestamped views, downloads, uploads, invitation/permission changes) is documented as visible ONLY to Owner/Manager/Collaborator; the sent-package Track report is sender-only ('only the sender (owner) can click Track'). Hypothesis: these read endpoints authorize on the caller's authentication plus the object's numeric ID but skip the per-object role check, so swapping in another folder_id or mail/package id yields another object's audit data to a Downloader/Uploader/Viewer or to a package recipient. Confirming behavior: test account B with Downloader on folder F retrieves the activity log for folder G (or a recipient of mail package P retrieves the Track table for package Q sent by someone else) using only the numeric ID, and receives the log contents. This is an IDOR on metadata, and metadata includes other users' emails, access times and IPs (per RECIPIENT TRACKING: recipient email, time of access, IP logged per download) — real confidentiality impact if exposed cross-object.
evidence: obs_diff n=33: 'Details tab ONLY to users holding Owner, Manager, or Collaborator privileges'; 'only the sender (owner) can click Track to see a table of which recipients opened the email, viewed attachments, or downloaded them'; obs_diff n=34: end users see only their own shared-folder activity vs admins seeing all. Accellion security FAQ: RECIPIENT TRACKING logs recipient email/time/IP.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) requesting the log/Track endpoint for an object where the caller lacks the required role returns 403/empty while succeeding for a privileged caller on the same object (per-object role check present); or (b) the endpoints are admin-only or sender-bound server-side (e.g., derived from the session, not from the supplied ID); or (c) IDs are unguessable and no grant path exists by which a low-role caller could learn another object's ID.

title: H4: 'Recipient Only' download endpoint validates token but not caller identity against recipient list
detail: Reference pattern: secure links are generated from a double 128-bit MD5 token (unguessable — so this is NOT a token-prediction claim); the object reference is the token plus, per the 'Recipient Only' model, a named recipient list. RECIPIENT VALIDATION — verifying the downloader is on the original recipient list, which prevents forwarded links from working — is documented as a System Administrator CONFIGURABLE OPTION, i.e., it can be OFF depending on deployment. Hypothesis: on the hunting environment, the download endpoint validates the link token (and expiry/download-count) but does NOT bind the authenticated caller's identity to the recipient list when recipient validation is disabled, so an authenticated identity B who was never a recipient can download a 'Recipient Only' file intended solely for A by using the token URL — equivalently, the endpoint may rely on 'anyone after authentication' semantics for links where 'Recipient Only' was intended. Confirming behavior: with two consenting test accounts, A creates a Recipient-Only share addressed to A's own other identity (or a controlled address), and B — an authenticated user never on the recipient list — successfully downloads the file via the token URL while only holding a valid session. This respects the program's validity bar ('bypass Recipient Only') and avoids the excluded 'anyone after authentication' class by testing only shares explicitly set to Recipient Only.
evidence: obs_diff n=25: 'SECURE LINK/URL: Generated by a double 128-bit MD5 token'; 'RECIPIENT VALIDATION: Accellion can verify if a user is on the original recipient list of the email for downloading a file. This prevents forwarding links. This is a System Administrators configurable option.'; program page (obs_app n=25): valid file disclosure must 'bypass "Recipient Only"'. obs_app n=25 handoff: 'token replay from a different authenticated identity' as the testable seam.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) identity B's download attempt with the token URL is rejected (403/login-wall mismatch) while the named recipient's attempt succeeds, showing caller-identity-to-recipient-list binding is enforced; or (b) the hunting environment has recipient validation enabled and the share creation UI does not permit Recipient-Only without it; or (c) the token URL forces a challenge (enter the exact recipient email + activation) that B cannot pass without controlling A's inbox.

title: CSRF via multipart form upload endpoints that skip token validation
detail: Kiteworks Core is a file-transfer platform; share/file-upload flows commonly use multipart/form-data. OPERATION: creating or modifying a share (e.g., set public-link, change share expiry, revoke access) or uploading a file into a share. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR (later, under authorization, on synthetic test data only): a cross-site form POST (multipart, no custom headers, no CSRF token) to the share-mutation endpoint, executed with the victim session's cookies, produces the state change that a same-origin request produces (share created/modified). The hypothesis holds if the endpoint accepts requests carrying only cookies and the Content-Type is one of the simple-request-compatible multipart types, with no request-bound token required.
evidence: World model confirms file sharing is the core surface; homepage HTML shows a React SPA (22 static JS bundles) implying browser-form-friendly endpoints. No token mechanism observed yet (no login performed, passive only). Class-level prior: file-transfer apps often exempt upload endpoints from token checks to support large resumable/chunked uploads via pluggable uploaders.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) all state-changing endpoints require a per-request CSRF token that is bound to the session and validated server-side (visible in SPA JS as an anti-CSRF header/token injected into every mutation); or (b) session cookies carry SameSite=Strict and the endpoint requires a custom header, so no cross-site request can carry auth at all.

title: SameSite-cookie gap on GET-modeled state changes (share acceptance / link activation)
detail: OPERATION: state changes modeled as GET requests — e.g., accepting a shared-file invitation, activating a public link, confirming an email-gateway action, or clicking a 'verify email' style link. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR (later, authorized): an authenticated cross-site top-level navigation (simple link or img/redirect chain) to the GET-modeled endpoint performs the state change. The hypothesis holds if the session cookie lacks SameSite=Strict (Lax or unspecified/default), because top-level GET navigations still send Lax cookies, and the endpoint does not verify Origin/Referer or require a token on GET.
evidence: SPA architecture observed; Kiteworks flows (shares, email gateway actions, data forms) are naturally link-driven and historically prone to GET-modeled actions. Program-excluded classes do not cover this. No Set-Cookie attributes inspected yet.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) passive inspection of Set-Cookie headers shows SameSite=Strict (or __Host- + Secure + Path=/ with Strict) on the session cookie; or (b) all state-changing actions require POST/PUT/DELETE with a custom header or token; or (c) server-side GET handlers are strictly read-only with no state mutation.

title: Pre-auth state-changing endpoints (share-request / data-form submission) missing token binding
detail: OPERATION: unauthenticated-but-session-bound state changes, e.g., submitting a Secure Data Form / Advanced Form, requesting access to a share, or triggering a password-reset email — endpoints that set a session cookie before authentication (pre-auth session). CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR (later, authorized): a cross-site request executed against a fresh pre-auth session completes the state change without any anti-CSRF token, because synchronizer tokens are often only issued post-login. The hypothesis holds if pre-auth session cookies exist and pre-auth mutation endpoints accept cookie-only requests.
evidence: World model lists Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms and share request flows as in-scope surface; these are inherently pre-auth entry points. Class-level prior: pre-auth flows are the most common place where token-based CSRF defense is absent by design.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) no session cookie is issued before authentication (all pre-auth endpoints are stateless); or (b) pre-auth mutation endpoints require a CAPTCHA, one-time token, or signed URL parameter that a cross-site attacker cannot obtain; or (c) pre-auth state changes are limited to email delivery with no security impact (rate-limit-excluded class).

title: Role parameter accepted on profile/update request
detail: If account-edit or profile-update endpoints accept a role/admin flag field in the request body, a normal user could promote themselves vertically by adding the field client-side. Check the API surface (agents 8/9) for PUT/PATCH user/profile routes and their accepted parameters.
evidence: Kiteworks bounty explicitly lists privilege/role escalation as high-value focus; profile-edit mass-assignment is a classic vertical-escalation primitive.
falsifier: Profile/account update requests reject or ignore extra role fields, and observed update requests contain no role-related parameter names.

title: Invitation flow grants requester-chosen role
detail: If share/invite endpoints let the inviter select a recipient role (editor, manager, admin) without server-side authorization check on the inviter's own privilege, a low-privilege user could invite a controlled second identity with an elevated role, then use that account to escalate.
evidence: Kiteworks is a file-sharing platform with invitation/share flows; invitation role-grant is a known privesc pattern in collaboration products.
falsifier: Invite endpoints either lack a role parameter, require the inviter to already hold the granted role, or server-side downgrade the granted role for unprivileged inviters.

title: Group-membership change lacks admin check
detail: If API endpoints for adding users to groups/folders accept a group id and user id without verifying the caller is a group admin, a user could add their own account to an admin/privileged group, inheriting its permissions.
evidence: World model open question #3 asks how permissions are modeled; group-based permission inheritance is standard in MFT/file-share products.
falsifier: Group-membership mutations return 403 for non-admin callers, or require a server-held admin token distinct from the caller identity.

title: Self-registration assigns elevated default role
detail: If the signup/registration flow accepts a role or group parameter, or defaults new accounts to a privileged role due to misconfiguration, vertical escalation is possible at account creation without any existing privileged account.
evidence: Hunting environment is a fresh YesWeHack instance; test environments are historically prone to permissive default-role misconfiguration.
falsifier: Registration responses and subsequent session tokens show only an unprivileged/default role, and role/group parameters are ignored in signup requests.

title: /adminRoles role-grant reachable by non-admin token (function-level check missing on privilege-mutating endpoint)
detail: ADMIN FUNCTION (per docs): /adminRoles assigns System/Application Administrator roles; documented invariant is that only a System Admin can designate administrators and users cannot self-promote (obs_app n18: '/adminRoles REST API requires authentication as an administrative user'). BFLA QUESTION: does the /adminRoles assignment endpoint (POST/PUT on a grant action) enforce the admin requirement, or does it only require *authentication*, letting any authenticated low-privileged caller (e.g., an external restricted user or internal non-admin) grant an admin role to their own account? CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR (in a future controlled test): a low-privilege bearer token submits the documented admin-role grant for its own user and receives success (2xx), and a subsequent /rest/users/me shows the admin role active/effective. NOT a self-XSS/rate-limit class; this is the program's explicitly-valued privilege-escalation seam.
evidence: obs_app n18: 'The /adminRoles REST API requires authentication as an administrative user' and 'only system administrators can designate users as administrators (including application administrators); users cannot promote themselves to system administrators'. obs_app n16: 'Admin user CRUD via /admin (list/add/update/delete users, settings, admin roles, profile image)'.
falsifier: A low-privileged token's role-grant call returns 401/403 consistently across grant verbs (POST/PUT/PATCH), and /rest/users/me shows no admin-role change afterward; or the endpoint 404s/is absent for non-admins in the hunting environment. Rejected if role listing is admin-gated but the *grant* action shares the same gate.

title: /profiles privilege-mutation callable by non-admin (profile bundle edit vs admin-gated read)
detail: ADMIN FUNCTION (per docs): /profiles manages privilege/feature bundles per user — the documented three-layer model makes User Profiles the vehicle for privilege assignment (obs_app n16: 'User Profiles (/profiles/) = feature/privilege bundles per user'). BFLA QUESTION: the /profiles endpoints may split into a readable list (possibly user-visible) and privilege-mutating writes. If the write path (PUT/PATCH on a profile, or assigning a profile to a user) lacks the admin function-level check while the surrounding reads are reachable, a non-admin could elevate their own privilege bundle. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: a low-privilege token mutates a profile (or its own profile assignment) and the privilege change takes effect on subsequent calls. Distinct from /adminRoles: this is the /profiles seam, the privilege-bundle layer beneath admin roles.
evidence: obs_app n16: 'Privileges are assigned via User Profiles; folder access via folder roles; admin power via admin roles' and '/profiles (manage privileges/features assigned to users)'; n18: 'The REST API exposes privilege-management endpoints: /profiles (manage privileges/features assigned to users) ... Per design, /adminRoles and privilege-mutating /profiles calls must reject non-admin callers; any such call succeeding with a low-privilege token is a vertical escalation.'
falsifier: Every privilege-mutating /profiles call (profile create/update, user-profile assignment) returns 401/403 with a low-privileged token, and only read-only profile listing (if any) is reachable; no privilege change observable after attempted writes. Rejected if profile writes are verified admin-gated end-to-end in the hunting environment.

title: Folder member role management allows Manager-to-Owner self-promotion or Owner demotion (variant of CVE-2025-53939)
detail: ADMIN/FUNCTION-LEVEL FUNCTION (per docs): folder role management is restricted — Owners and Managers manage users/stakeholders and assign roles, but documentation leaves open whether a Manager can promote themselves to Owner or demote the Owner (obs_app n19 open question #3). CVE-2025-53939 (pre-9.1.0) proved this exact code path — shared-folder role management — produced real unexpected privilege elevation, so a 9.5.1 variant (e.g., a downgrade-then-upgrade transition, stale role caching, or a role-id parameter on /rest/folders/{id} member APIs) is the highest-value BFLA variant. BFLA QUESTION: does the member role-update function check that the caller holds a sufficient role (Owner) to *change* roles, or does a Manager/Collaborator token succeed in altering membership roles including its own? CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: a Manager (or Collaborator) token updates its own folder membership role to Owner — or demotes the current Owner — and the change is effective on subsequent folder access (e.g., previously-blocked owner-only operations now succeed).
evidence: obs_app n19: 'Shared-folder role management is a historically bug-dense surface (CVE-2025-53939): Prior to 9.1.0, improper input validation when managing roles of a shared folder allowed unexpected elevation of another user's permissions on the share.' Also n19 open questions: '(3) Can a Manager promote themselves to Owner, or demote the Owner?' Folder role ladder documented n18/n25 (Viewer < Downloader < Uploader < Collaborator < Manager < Owner).
falsifier: Role-update calls by Manager/Collaborator tokens return 403 (or are ignored), effective folder role of the caller never changes, and no Owner-demotion is possible; i.e., only the current Owner can mutate membership roles. Rejected if the hunting env's member APIs are read-only for non-owners, or if role-id parameters are strictly validated against caller authority.

title: /admin/devices/ remote-wipe or device management callable across users by non-admin token
detail: ADMIN FUNCTION (per docs): /admin/devices/ gives administrators device management including remote wipe of other users' devices (obs_app n16: 'Per-user device tracking with remote wipe (/devices/, /admin/devices/)'). The intended boundary is: a user may manage their OWN devices via /devices/, while /admin/devices/ requires admin authority to act on ANY device. BFLA QUESTION: does the /admin/devices/ wipe/manage function enforce admin identity, or does any authenticated token reach a cross-user device operation (missing function-level check on the admin device path)? CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: a non-admin token issues a remote-wipe (or device-state change) against a DIFFERENT user's device via the /admin/devices/ path and receives success (2xx), with the state change reflected on the target device record — a destructive-integrity impact against another user, distinct from self-device management. Note: testing must use the researcher's own second test identity only; wiping any real user's device would violate program rules.
evidence: obs_app n16: 'Identity extends to devices and external content sources — Per-user device tracking with remote wipe (/devices/, /admin/devices/)' and 'Admin user CRUD via /admin (list/add/update/delete users, settings, admin roles, profile image)'.
falsifier: Cross-user device operations via /admin/devices/ return 401/403 for non-admin tokens while /devices/ only operates on the caller's own devices; or the /admin/devices/ path is entirely absent for non-admin callers in the hunting environment. Rejected if a second test identity's device cannot be touched by the first test identity's token.

title: H1: roleId on POST /rest/folders/{id}/members not clamped to inviter's privilege
detail: The documented member-add call takes a userId+roleId payload where roleId is a small numeric enum (e.g. downloader=2; GET /rest/roles enumerates them). Hypothesis: the endpoint binds roleId directly into the membership record and only checks that the caller may add members, but does NOT clamp the granted roleId to roles at-or-below the caller's own role. A caller holding Uploader/Downloader could then add a controlled second identity (or themselves) with roleId=Manager/Owner. Confirming behavior (later, under authorization, two consenting test accounts): account B with low role on a folder POSTs /rest/folders/{F}/members with userId of a second test identity and roleId of the Owner/Manager enum, the call returns success, and a subsequent GET members listing shows the new identity holding the elevated role — an effective vertical grant, not a UI cosmetic.
evidence: obs_diff: 'API: POST /rest/folders/{id}/members with userId+roleId payload'; 'adding a contact with roleId; GET /rest/roles enumerates roles'; old Accellion REST 'used numeric roleId (downloader=2) via /rest/folders/{id}'; role ladder Viewer/Uploader/Downloader vs Collaborator/Manager/Owner (obs_app n=18/n=19). Program lists privilege/role escalation as high-value.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) a low-role caller's member-add with a high roleId is rejected (403) or silently clamped to the caller's own role or below, verified in the members listing; or (b) member-add is rejected for all non-Owner/non-Manager callers regardless of roleId; or (c) roleId values outside the caller's grant are not bindable because the enum is validated server-side against the caller's role.

title: H2: Guarded user attributes bindable on user update endpoint (admin/user flags via PUT /rest/users/{id})
detail: The admin REST API documents list/add/update/delete users (ref /rest/index.html). Hypothesis: the update-user endpoint deserializes the full request body into the user model, so a request that legitimately updates benign profile fields can also carry guarded attributes (e.g. an admin flag, userType/system role, or admin-role assignment) and have them persisted. Confirming behavior (later, under authorization, two consenting test accounts, ResearchSession-gated): an update request on test account B's own record including a guarded attribute returns success and the attribute persists in GET /rest/users/{id} or /rest/users/me, changing B's effective privilege. This is distinct from the self-registration variant (agent 56 H4) — it targets the update path, where session-bound model binding is most likely to include sensitive setters.
evidence: obs_app: 'admin REST API endpoints for list/add/update/delete users' documented at /rest/index.html; obs_diff: '/adminRoles requires aut...' and separate System Admin vs Application Admin vs End User namespaces, implying role fields exist in the user model. Class-level prior: PUT-binding of privileged fields is the canonical mass-assignment pattern.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) the update endpoint rejects or silently strips non-documented/unguarded attributes (verified: GET shows no change and, where visible, a 400 on unknown fields); or (b) the field whitelist is documented in /rest/index.html and contains no privilege fields; or (c) the endpoint is unreachable for non-admin sessions at all (403 before body processing).

title: H3: ownerId bindable on folder create/update (POST/PUT /rest/folders{/{id}}) enabling ownership reassignment
detail: Hypothesis: folder create/update endpoints bind an owner identifier field (ownerId/owner/userId or similar) from the request body rather than deriving ownership solely from the session. If so, a low-privileged user could create a folder nominally owned by another identity, or — more impactfully — update a folder's owner field to take or transfer ownership, inheriting owner-only capabilities (member add/remove, activity-log visibility). Confirming behavior (later, under authorization, synthetic test data): creating a folder with an explicit ownerId body field and observing the Details view / folder metadata reflecting the supplied owner rather than the creator; or a non-owner update call succeeding in changing the owner field. Must be distinguished from delegation flows where ownership transfer is an explicit, authorized feature.
evidence: obs_app: 'role-id handling in /rest/folders/{id} member APIs, downgrade-then-upgrade transitions' flagged as variant surface on 9.5.1; obs_diff: folder Details/activity log 'ONLY to users holding Owner, Manager, or Collaborator privileges' — ownership confers restricted visibility, so its binding is high-value. Numeric sequential object IDs (id: 1240) make ownership fields addressable.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) folder create/update ignores a supplied owner field (metadata shows creator as owner, 200 without effect) or rejects it (400); or (b) only an existing Owner/Manager can invoke the ownership field and the transfer is an explicitly authorized delegation flow; or (c) the endpoint binds no such field — owner derived from session in all observed requests.

title: H4: Extra permission flags bindable on share creation (canReshare/role beyond documented enum on secure-file/mail share)
detail: Secure-file and mail share endpoints take permission parameters (share-level roles/permissions such as view vs download, recipient lists, expiry). Hypothesis: the share-create call binds additional undocumented permission flags from the body — e.g. a reshare/canShare boolean, an 'admin' permission value outside the documented enum, or a recipient-capability override — so a caller restricted to creating view-only shares can mint a share whose recipient holds broader rights than the caller is entitled to grant. Confirming behavior (later, under authorization, two consenting test accounts): test account A creates a share for test account B with an extra flag in the create payload; B's observed capabilities (download, reshare, recipient management) exceed the documented grant A is permitted to make, verified by B exercising the capability against the share.
evidence: obs_diff: 'Recipient Only' recipient-list model and RECIPIENT VALIDATION as admin-configurable option show share payloads carry capability-relevant fields; obs_app: share/permission model is an open research question (world-model Q3). Class-level prior: share-creation endpoints in collaboration products frequently bind permission booleans client-side.
falsifier: Rejected if: (a) the create response omits the extra flag and B's capabilities match only the documented grant; or (b) the endpoint validates the permission parameter against a strict enum and rejects unknown values/flags (400); or (c) recipient capabilities are derived server-side from the caller's own grant, never from caller-supplied flags.

title: Content-Type sniffing mismatch on uploaded previews/download
detail: Upload pipeline accepts a file with a benign declared content-type (e.g. image/png) whose body is actually HTML/JS; when the recipient opens it inline via the sharing link, the app serves it with attacker-influenced Content-Type (or omits Content-Disposition: attachment and nosniff), enabling stored XSS on a kiteworks.dev origin. Weakness is in the render/preview-serving layer, not the AV gate.
evidence: None yet — passive dossier only; world model open question #3 asks how upload/share flows work. Kiteworks is a file-sharing product where inline preview is a core feature.
falsifier: Manual test shows downloaded/previewed files are always served with Content-Disposition: attachment and/or X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff + a sanitized generic type, so inline script execution on the origin is impossible.

title: Archive nested-payload smuggling past AV/preview pipeline
detail: Upload pipeline decompresses archives (zip/7z) for preview or AV scanning; a nested or malformed archive (e.g. zip-within-zip, non-standard compression method, or zip slip-style entry name containing ../) is either not scanned recursively or, when extracted server-side for preview, writes outside the intended temp dir. Note: program excludes AV bypass by mere renaming, but a traversal in the server-side extraction layer is a distinct path-traversal class, not rename-bypass.
evidence: No direct evidence yet; inference from product class — Kiteworks MFT historically handles archives, and preview generators commonly decompress server-side.
falsifier: Manual test: upload a nested archive with a benign tracer entry (zip-slip-style name) and confirm (a) it is rejected or sanitized, or (b) any server-side extraction confines entries to the sandbox temp dir — e.g. the tracer never appears outside its container and no error discloses paths.

title: Preview-generator SSRF/XSLT-style transformation on uploaded documents
detail: Document preview/thumbnail generation (PDF, office docs, images) invokes a server-side converter; a crafted document containing external-entity references (e.g. XXE in DOCX/SVG) or external resource references triggers the converter to make outbound requests or expose file contents in the rendered preview. This is a transformation-layer injection, distinct from AV bypass.
evidence: None yet — purely hypothesis; Kiteworks' preview feature is standard for secure file-sharing platforms and converters (ImageMagick/LibreOffice class) historically carry XXE/SSRF risks.
falsifier: Manual test: upload an SVG/DOCX with an external-entity probe to a collaborator DNS you control (or a harmless internal marker); if the generated preview returns no external callback/content and the converter is configured with external entities disabled, hypothesis is falsified.

title: Trusted-device ('Remember this device') marker suppresses 2FA on sensitive flows without device binding
detail: Bypass path: the documented 'Remember this device' option sets a device-trust marker that suppresses the second-factor prompt on subsequent logins. If the marker is not cryptographically bound to a device fingerprint (stored server-side and validated), a stolen or copied marker would skip 2FA for the account; further, if the marker also suppresses step-up verification inside privileged flows (role/admin changes, API-token issuance), the attacker inherits full session authority without ever touching a second factor. Confirming behavior: (a) a remember-device cookie/localStorage marker accepted across different browsers/machines without re-prompt; (b) no server-side binding (marker is a plain flag or opaque value not tied to fingerprint); (c) sensitive in-session actions proceed with only the marker, no fresh 2FA. Manual-test only, single benign session, no other accounts.
evidence: obs #43: Getting Started Guide documents 'Remember this device' trusted-device option; obs #28: admin-configured 2FA (RADIUS or email OTP). No evidence yet on marker format, binding, or step-up behavior — purely hypothesis.
falsifier: The remember-device marker is a signed/encrypted opaque token bound server-side to a device fingerprint, rotated per device, and privileged/sensitive actions re-trigger 2FA (step-up) regardless of the marker; or the marker only affects the login prompt and nothing beyond it.

title: First-to-enroll wins on self-provisioned accounts: invite recipient's 2FA can be bound by an interceptor
detail: Bypass path: self-provisioning is invite-triggered (obs #16: invite -> create account with matching email -> email passcode 2FA). If the 2FA enrollment step (authenticator binding / mobile OTP registration) is not session-bound to the exact session that completed the verified email step, someone holding the invite link/email (interception, mailbox rule, shared inbox) could enroll their own second factor on the new account before the legitimate recipient completes setup, permanently owning the account's 2FA. Confirming behavior: enrollment endpoint accepts only the invite token/email identity and permits authenticator/device binding without continuity from the original verified session. Falsifier: enrollment requires the live authenticated session of the verified account holder and cannot be initiated, resumed, or rebound from a fresh session; enrollment must complete within the same session that verified the email.
evidence: obs #16 (high): 9-step self-provisioning flow ends with 'email passcode 2FA' at account creation; optional mobile OTP. Enrollment-vs-session binding not documented — hypothesis only.
falsifier: 2FA enrollment is strictly bound to the session that completed email verification (same session, short window, single-shot), and any enrollment attempt from a new session requires full re-authentication including the account password.

title: Recovery/backup-code regeneration without step-up re-authentication
detail: Bypass path: an attacker with a valid session (stolen cookie, shared workstation) can view or regenerate 2FA recovery/backup codes without supplying the current password or passing a fresh 2FA challenge, thereby converting a session-only compromise into permanent 2FA-free access and locking out the legitimate user's recovery path. Confirming behavior: the recovery-code view/regenerate endpoint accepts a session cookie alone (no password re-entry, no fresh OTP); regeneration invalidates the user's existing codes silently. Manual single-session test only, test account only. Falsifier: endpoint requires step-up (current password + fresh 2FA verification) before displaying or regenerating codes, and regeneration notifies the user via out-of-band channel.
evidence: No recovery-code flow is documented in the collected observations; absence of evidence either way. Email-OTP-based 2FA (obs #28) implies an email-dependent recovery path that may be weakly gated. Hypothesis is speculative until the account-settings surface is mapped.
falsifier: Recovery/backup codes, if they exist, require current-password re-entry plus a fresh second-factor verification before display or regeneration, and regeneration triggers an out-of-band notification to the account owner.

title: 2FA identity confusion via configurable 'LDAP Username Attribute'
detail: Bypass path: 2FA for directory users is configured via RADIUS or built-in email OTP with an admin-chosen 'LDAP Username Attribute' (obs #28). If the 2FA challenge identity resolution keys off this configurable attribute rather than the directory's immutable object ID, and the attribute is non-unique (e.g., mail, or an attribute that collides across entries), a user whose controlled attribute value matches another account's attribute could cause the OTP challenge to be issued against / resolved to the wrong directory identity — weakening second-factor binding for LDAP users. Confirming behavior: challenge request takes a username, resolves it via the configured attribute, and attribute collisions (or alternate-attribute lookups) change which account the OTP is issued for. No enumeration or attribute probing — test only with known test identities and observable challenge routing. Falsifier: challenge resolution always keys off the directory's immutable object identifier (objectGUID/entryUUID) regardless of the configured username attribute, and the attribute is validated as unique at configuration time.
evidence: obs #28 (high): deployment checklist shows auth types AD/LDAP, SSO, self-registration, manual entry; 2FA options Radius or built-in email OTP with dedicated 'LDAP Username Attribute' field tying OTP/auth to a directory attribute. No evidence on resolution key uniqueness — hypothesis only.
falsifier: The 2FA challenge resolution key is the immutable directory object ID (not the configurable username attribute), the attribute is enforced unique, or directory users authenticate through a different, non-attributable path.

title: Mobile-variant OAuth authorize (m=1) path skips or weakens a check the web login enforces
detail: Bypass path: authenticate through /oauth/authorize?m=1 (documented mobile-friendly authorization page variant) using a registered mobile OAuth client_id/secret, instead of the standard web login flow. Mobile apps are described in vendor docs as registered OAuth custom applications (client_id/secret/scopes), i.e., a distinct auth pipeline is reachable. Confirming behavior: obtaining an authorization code/access token via the m=1 variant (or via a mobile client registration) while one of the web flow's verifications (2FA step, consent screen, or device-trust gate) is not enforced on that variant. Falsifier: the m=1 page renders through the identical auth pipeline with the same mandatory 2FA/consent/device checks — i.e., both variants behave identically and mobile-client registrations cannot skip any web-flow verification.
evidence: obs_diff.jsonl n43: '/oauth/authorize accepts an m parameter set to 1 to display a mobile-friendly authorization page'; 'Mobile apps are described as registered OAuth custom applications (client_id/secret/scopes)'; web 2FA includes 'Remember this device' trusted-device option while mobile lists RADIUS 2FA/MFA + native OTP — distinct option sets per client type.
falsifier: Code/request inspection shows the m=1 page and standard page share one auth-pipeline implementation, and both enforce the same mandatory 2FA, consent, and device checks (no step present in web is absent in mobile variant).

title: SAML SP accepts an unsigned or signature-confused assertion (SimpleSAMLphp ACS)
detail: Bypass path: submit a SAML response to the SP's ACS endpoint /sp/module.php/saml/sp/saml2-acs.php/sp-sso in which the Assertion (or the Response) lacks a valid signature, or the signature covers only an unsigned wrapper while the asserted identity comes from an unsigned inner element. Confirming behavior: the SP mints an authenticated session for the attacker-controlled identity from a response/assertion that the IdP never signed. Falsifier: the SP configuration requires valid signatures on both Response and Assertion for all inbound assertions, rejects unsigned assertions outright, and never trusts an unsigned inner element (verifiable from SimpleSAMLphp authsources/metadata config or observed rejection of an unsigned assertion).
evidence: obs_app.jsonl n28: Microsoft Entra SSO tutorial gives ACS URL pattern https://<kiteworksURL>/sp/module.php/saml/sp/saml2-acs.php/sp-sso — SimpleSAMLphp's canonical SAML SP endpoint; observation notes SimpleSAMLphp's known vulnerability history (signature handling, XML parsing). obs_app.jsonl n28: SSO Setup exposes SP Entity ID / signed AuthnRequests / RSA cert toggles, i.e., signature policy is admin-configurable and may be mis-set.
falsifier: SSO metadata/config review or live probe of a signed-only policy shows every inbound assertion requires a valid IdP signature (unsigned/invalidly-signed assertions are rejected with an error), so there is no signature-validation gap to bypass.

title: Just-in-time SSO provisioning merges attacker-controlled IdP attributes into an existing (victim) account
detail: Bypass path: as an identity able to assert attributes through the configured IdP (SP-initiated SSO with JIT provisioning), supply a NameID or directory attribute (e.g., email/sAMAccountName) that matches an existing privileged Kiteworks account, causing JIT provisioning to link/merge into the victim's account instead of creating a fresh one. Confirming behavior: a fresh SSO login with an attacker-controlled IdP identity results in a session bound to an existing victim account (visible as the victim's profile/folders/permissions). Falsifier: JIT provisioning only ever creates new accounts and never merges into existing ones; existing-identity linkage requires an explicit, admin-verified identity-linking action outside the SSO assertion path.
evidence: obs_app.jsonl n28 (IdP-assigned users may get access without a pre-existing Kiteworks account; 'Implies just-in-time provisioning driven by IdP assertion attributes — trust boundary: IdP-supplied attributes create/authorize accounts'); obs_app.jsonl n16 (SP-initiated SSO + JIT user provisioning; accounts auto-created on first SSO login); obs_app.jsonl n28 (LDAP attributes drive automatic provisioning and profile/role assignment — attribute values map to profiles/privileges).
falsifier: Provisioning logic review or live test shows the IdP-to-Kiteworks identity mapping only creates new accounts (or fails on collision) and cannot link an IdP assertion to a different pre-existing local account without admin-verified identity linking.

title: 'Recipient Only' share readable by an unauthenticated party via the recipient self-registration flow
detail: Bypass path: for a 'Recipient Only' secure share, the external recipient flow requires clicking 'Access Message', entering the recipient email, and — if unregistered — setting a password via an activation email; identity proof is control of the recipient's inbox. The hypothesis is that the registration/activation step does not actually require inbox control (e.g., the activation token or link is predictable, reusable, or the flow falls back to 'anyone after authentication'), so an unauthenticated party can register under the recipient's address and read the share. Confirming behavior: registering the recipient's address without receiving/clicking the inbox activation email still yields an authenticated session that can view the 'Recipient Only' content. Falsifier: the flow requires clicking a single-use, unguessable activation link delivered to the recipient's inbox before any share content renders — i.e., no path reaches the share without demonstrated inbox control.
evidence: obs_app.jsonl n25: 'External recipient flow: click Access Message in email -> enter the SAME email address the message was sent to -> if unregistered, set a password and create an account -> activation email -> activate -> inbox with download link. Identity proof is: control of the recipient email inbox. No out-of-band identity verification in the default flow.' obs_app.jsonl n25 handoff: recipient validation is an admin-configurable OPTION; the program draws the validity line at bypassing 'Recipient Only'.
falsifier: Registration flow review or live test shows the activation token is single-use, unguessable, bound to the recipient address, and mandatory before any share content is visible, with no fallback that lets a non-recipient complete registration.

title: OAuth JWT algorithm confusion on bearer-token validation (none/HS256 against RS256)
detail: Weakness: the documented /oauth/authorize authorization-code flow issues bearer tokens to registered custom applications; many enterprise deployments use JWT access tokens, and a resource server that supports RS256 but also falls back to unverified 'none' or HS256 is a classical confusion primitive. HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization, on owned tokens only): decode a self-issued access token to learn its alg/kid claims, then present modified variants (alg switched to none, alg switched to HS256 signed with the published public key, tampered kid) against a protected /rest/* endpoint in the same session scope. The OBSERVED BEHAVIOR that would confirm: a mutated token (e.g., alg=none) is accepted and authorizes API calls exactly like the legitimate token, showing the server does not pin the algorithm to the issuer's signing key. This is a validation bug, not token forgery against another user.
evidence: obs_app n43: Kiteworks uses an OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow ('/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&response_type=code&scope=&redirect_uri=...'), and every API integration requires a registered custom application with client_id/secret — so server-issued tokens exist. Token FORMAT has not been observed (no token captured passively); alg confusion applies only if access tokens are JWTs. Class-level prior only.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) access tokens are opaque reference tokens (server-side lookup) rather than JWTs — alg confusion is then structurally impossible; or (b) token validation strictly pins RS256 with the issuer key and rejects any alg/kid mismatch (mutated tokens return 401/403 consistently); or (c) mutated tokens only fail gracefully with identical 401 responses and no differential.

title: Chunked-upload session tokens not bound to folder/user scope (initiateUpload session reuse)
detail: Weakness: the chunked upload flow mints an upload-session identifier via POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload (or /files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload) that authorizes subsequent chunk PUTs. If that session token is treated as a standalone bearer capability without server-side binding to the originating folder id and user, a session minted for folder F could address folder G. HOW tested (later, under authorization, with two owned folders): initiate an upload session in owned folder F, then attempt to address the returned session token against owned folder G (or vice versa) and observe. The OBSERVED BEHAVIOR that would confirm: the server accepts chunk data under the F-minted session token when pointed at G, showing the session token carries authority independent of the folder it was issued for.
evidence: obs_app n22/n41: upload-session mechanics documented (initiateUpload for new file and new version, session-like upload workflow with totalChunks/lastChunk). Binding of the session ID to folder/user is not described anywhere in the docs reviewed — neither confirmed nor denied. Class-level prior: upload-session IDs are a recurring under-scoped capability token in file apps.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) chunk endpoints re-derive folder/user authorization server-side from the session ID record and return 403 when the session's folder does not match the addressed folder; or (b) session IDs are single-use per folder and unguessable AND checked against the caller's session on every chunk; or (c) the hunting environment does not expose the session ID to the client at all (server tracks it internally).

title: Qualified-link expiry not enforced server-side; standard secure links may have no expiry at all
detail: Weakness: secure links are generated from a double 128-bit MD5 token (unguessable, so this is NOT a prediction claim); qualified links add an admin-configurable lifespan. The documented seam is that lifespan is admin-CONFIGURABLE (may be off/unset) and enforcement location (server vs client/UI) is not documented. HOW tested (later, under authorization, on own shares only): create a qualified link with a short lifespan, let it expire, then re-request the token URL and observe the raw download endpoint response. The OBSERVED BEHAVIOR that would confirm: an expired qualified link's token URL still returns 200 with file bytes (expiry enforced only in UI or not at all), or standard (non-qualified) secure links demonstrably have no expiry parameter and survive past any documented maximum. Missing expiry on bearer download tokens is a token-lifetime weakness regardless of token entropy.
evidence: obs_app n25: 'SECURE LINK/URL: Generated by a double 128-bit MD5 token'; 'QUALIFIED LINK/URL: The link has a limited lifespan (configurable by the System Administrator)'; recipient validation is also 'configurable'. Enforcement point (server-side check vs UI-only) is not documented. Class-level prior: link expiry is frequently enforced in the frontend or only at link-generation time.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) an expired qualified link's token URL returns 403/expired consistently across the raw endpoint and UI; or (b) standard secure links are shown to have a default maximum lifespan enforced server-side even when the admin leaves the setting unset; or (c) expiry state is checked on every download request via a server-side timestamp comparison.

title: OAuth refresh tokens / custom-application API tokens / 'remember this device' tokens survive account disable or password change
detail: Weakness: token revocation on credential/session lifecycle events (password change, account deactivation) is the classic session-management gap. Precedent exists in this product family: CVE-2026-29092 showed EPG sessions surviving account disable pre-9.2.1. The hunting environment runs 9.5.1, so the question is whether the FIX was complete across ALL token classes — OAuth refresh tokens, registered custom-application API tokens, upload-session tokens, and 'remember this device' trusted-device tokens — or only for the EPG session class that was reported. HOW tested (later, under authorization, on own test accounts only): issue tokens of each class for test account B, disable B (or change its password) from a separate admin/owned identity, then attempt to use each token class and observe. The OBSERVED BEHAVIOR that would confirm: one or more token classes continue to authorize API/download calls after disable/password-change, showing revocation was class-specific rather than global.
evidence: obs_diff n19: CVE-2026-29092 — EPG sessions could survive account disable pre-9.2.1 (patched). obs_app n43: 'Remember this device' trusted-device option exists (a long-lived token class); OAuth custom-application tokens exist (n43). No documentation found describing a global token-revocation invariant on disable/password change. Class-level prior: revocation fixes routinely cover only the reported token class.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) after disable/password-change, every token class (OAuth refresh, custom-app API token, upload-session token, remember-device token) fails authorization consistently; or (b) the hunting environment does not expose a path to disable an owned account and re-test, making this untestable here; or (c) tokens are short-lived with no refresh path so the residual window is negligible (then it is a low-impact lifetime note, not a weakness).

title: H64-1: PHP object injection via SimpleSAMLphp-based SAML SP session handling
detail: Integration observations (agent 28) indicate Kiteworks Core's SAML 2.0 service-provider implementation is SimpleSAMLphp-based (PHP). PHP session serialization is a classic unserialize() sink: SimpleSAMLphp stores serialized session/auth state (memcache, file, or DB-backed session store) and unserializes it on subsequent requests. Entry point: SAML endpoints — /saml2 AssertionConsumerService and /simplesaml/* module URLs on the hunting host. Confirming behavior: malformed SAMLResponse values produce distinct error paths (base64/gzip XML parse errors vs PHP unserialize warnings such as 'unserialize(): Error at offset'), or session-state-dependent behavior differences when session storage is tampered at the transport layer. Note: Kiteworks history includes PHP-based components, consistent with this stack signal.
evidence: obs: agent 28 'SAML 2.0 SP appears to be SimpleSAMLphp-based'; agent 14: /login_config script reference in SPA (may reveal enabled SSO integrations); Kiteworks is known for PHP heritage components
falsifier: Direct requests to /simplesaml/* and SAML metadata endpoints return 404/absent (SimpleSAMLphp not deployed on this instance); or /login_config shows SAML disabled and the auth flow uses a non-PHP identity library with strict typed session stores. If sessions never pass through PHP unserialize, this hypothesis is dead.

title: H64-2: Insecure deserialization in REST import/export of Secure Data Forms / workflow definitions
detail: Kiteworks Secure Data Forms and the MFT 'flow engine' involve user-imported structured definitions (form schemas, workflow/process definitions, branding packages) that must be deserialized server-side into executable structures (field expressions, validation rules, flow steps). Entry point: /rest/* import endpoints and the SDF form-import UI flow (JSON/XML definition uploads). Confirming behavior: imported definitions containing typed/nested structures (e.g., explicit class or type annotations, expression fields with server-side evaluation semantics) elicit type-coercion errors or evaluation behavior distinct from plain schema-validation rejections. Related: historical pre-9.2.0 arbitrary-upload CVEs show this pipeline has had input-handling flaws.
evidence: obs: agents 22/25 — SDF forms + MFT flow designer with import flows; historical CVEs (pre-9.2.0 arbitrary upload, SDF unrestricted dangerous-type upload); WORLD_MODEL open question 4 (API surface)
falsifier: Imported definitions are validated against a strict allowlist JSON schema / XSD with zero class instantiation or expression evaluation server-side; all formula/expression logic runs client-side only. If every import path rejects type-annotated payloads identically to malformed JSON, there is no deserialization sink.

title: H64-3: Token/session deserialization flaw in the MCP server OAuth callback flow
detail: The Kiteworks MCP server (github.com/kiteworks/mcp) implements OAuth with a localhost-callback flow (http://localhost:9999/callback) and grants scoped access to AI clients. Token exchange and session claim handling deserialize untrusted structured data (authorization codes, state parameters, claim blobs). Entry point: MCP OAuth endpoints and the localhost:9999/callback exchange. Confirming behavior: type-confused token payloads (e.g., numeric-vs-string claim types, nested objects where a flat string is expected) produce decoder/coercion errors instead of clean signature-validation failures. Falsifier: tokens are signed JWTs whose signature is verified before any claim decoding, and no opaque serialized blobs are ever decoded server-side.
evidence: obs: agent 14 — MCP OAuth app docs (docs via github.com/kiteworks/mcp), localhost:9999/callback flow; AI Data Gateway trust-boundary note
falsifier: MCP server uses JWS-only tokens with strict pre-verification and no pickle/serialize-style decoding of any untrusted blob; callback parameters are plain strings. If the code path shows signature-first verification, the hypothesis fails.

title: H64-4: S/MIME and PKCS#7 envelope parsing in the Email Protection Gateway as a deserialization sink
detail: The EPG 'Data Policy Engine' parses complex serialized structures in the mail stream: S/MIME, OpenPGP, DKIM/DMARC, and client-applied MIP sensitivity labels — all ASN.1/DER or structured-token formats. Email-triggered flows bridge EPG into Core (large attachments via Outlook plugin). Entry point: inbound messages through the gateway into the hunting environment. Confirming behavior: malformed PKCS#7/S/MIME envelopes or crafted MIP label structures produce parser-specific failures (ASN.1 decode errors, padding-oracle-like timing/error differences) rather than clean spam/quarantine rejections. Falsifier: the hunting environment does not expose a live EPG inbound mail path to test accounts, or envelope parsing is delegated to a hardened library with no attacker-reachable object instantiation.
evidence: obs: agent 28 — EPG parses S/MIME, OpenPGP, DKIM/DMARC, MIP labels; email-triggered file flows bridge EPG and Core
falsifier: No EPG mail-receiving capability is reachable in scope for the hunting environment (out of scope or untestable), or parsing uses strict DER validation with no code-execution-capable deserialization step. Unreachable sink = rejected for this experiment.

title: SAML RelayState open redirect through SimpleSAMLphp SP ACS path
detail: The hunting environment uses SimpleSAMLphp-style SP endpoints (/sp/module.php/saml/... ACS path per agent #14). RelayState is the standard SAML carrier for post-login destination URLs and is attacker-influenced: an SP-initiated login request can carry an arbitrary RelayState value. INPUT: the RelayState parameter on the SP's login/initiate endpoint (and on the SAMLRequest redirect binding). HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): initiate the SSO flow with RelayState set to a canary external URL and observe where the session lands after authentication completes (or after the IdP interaction, using consenting test accounts). CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: after successful authentication the browser lands on the attacker-supplied external URL, proving the SP redirects to an unvalidated RelayState. CHAIN POTENTIAL: an unvalidated RelayState is the classic SSO phishing enabler and can also chain with the MCP Server OAuth localhost:9999 callback model (9.5+) if authorization-code flows pass through the same redirect handling. CONFIRMATION requires the external landing to be reproducible and attributable to RelayState (not to an IdP-configured default landing).
evidence: Agent #14: 'SAML 2.0 SSO (SimpleSAMLphp-style /sp/module.php/saml/... ACS path; IdPs incl. Entra ID/ADFS, Ping Identity)'; world model open question #5 asks where the LDAP/SSO integration points are — this is that integration point. SimpleSAMLphp historically redirects to RelayState without strict validation when not configured with a return-URL allowlist; untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the SP rejects non-whitelisted RelayState values (error page or forced default landing) for an external canary across repeated trials; or (b) RelayState is verified against a signed request or session-bound target before redirect; or (c) the hunting environment has no SSO login path enabled (local-auth only), making RelayState unreachable.

title: Login ?next=/?returnUrl= parameter honored as absolute external URL after authentication
detail: Enterprise login pages commonly accept a post-login destination (?next=, ?returnUrl=, ?redirect=, ?return_to=) so a session-timeout bounce can return the user to the protected page. INPUT: the destination query parameter on the Core login page (and on the session-timeout redirect to /login). HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): request the login page with the parameter set to a canary external URL, then complete a login with a consenting test account and observe the final 302/location target. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: post-login the browser receives a 302 to (or renders through) the exact attacker-supplied external URL, with the session still attached — i.e., the parameter is copied into the redirect without host allowlisting. CHAIN POTENTIAL: combined with any session-identifier-in-URL feature (e.g., share-link tokens, email-gateway one-time links) a redirect can carry bearer tokens to an external host in the Referer/Location; it is also the standard phishing landing that inherits the program's real trust domain. CONFIRMATION requires the external 302 to be reproducible across sessions and not a one-off error path.
evidence: World model: SPA shell at / references /login_config (auth configuration surface, full body fetch hangs — needs browser-rendered fetch by an eligible agent); agent #49 (reflected-xss) independently hypothesized redirect params (?next=/?returnUrl=/?redirect=) exist on auth pages. Untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the parameter is validated to relative paths only (external canary is replaced by a default landing page, consistently, across trials); or (b) no destination parameter exists on the login flow (post-login always lands on a fixed dashboard); or (c) the value is reflected only in-page with proper encoding and never used as a redirect target (302 Location never contains the external host).

title: Logout/SLO redirect parameter (logout?redirect= / SAML single-logout ReturnTo) issued as unvalidated 302
detail: Logout endpoints and SAML single-logout flows frequently accept a post-logout landing (?redirect=, ?returnTo=, ?next=, or SAML LogoutResponse Destination) so the IdP/SP can return the user to a branded page. INPUT: the post-logout destination parameter on the Core logout URL and on any SAML SLO endpoint. HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): issue an authenticated logout with the parameter set to a canary external URL and inspect the 302 Location chain. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: the server answers with a 302 to the exact external canary URL, proving the logout redirect is unvalidated. CHAIN POTENTIAL: this is the lowest-value redirect alone, but it matters as a redirector gadget — a logout URL under the trusted kiteworks domain that bounces to arbitrary external hosts is a standard payload-delivery primitive in phishing chains, and it can be combined with the RelayState vector (H1) for multi-hop chains that inherit the program's domain trust. CONFIRMATION requires the external 302 to be the documented response to the parameter, reproducible, and not issued by an intermediary (proxy/CDN).
evidence: World model: SSO/SAML integrations (Entra ID/ADFS, Ping Identity) per agent #14, which implies SLO/logout endpoints exist; 'Auto Redirect IP or Range forcing SSO by source IP' (obs_app n28) shows the platform already implements redirect-on-condition logic. Untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) logout ignores the parameter (always lands on a fixed page) or validates it to relative/same-origin paths; or (b) the SAML SLO flow requires a signed request carrying the return URL, so no attacker-settable parameter exists; or (c) no logout/SLO endpoint is reachable in the hunting environment.

title: Zip-slip in server-side archive extraction (uploaded archives)
detail: Kiteworks MFT handles file transfer flows that ingest archives; archive previews and automation workflows extract ZIP entries server-side. INPUT: archive entry names (the most likely path-flavored attacker input) inside an archive uploaded through a legitimate file flow. Confirming behavior (future authorized test with synthetic data only): an entry name containing '../' or an absolute path materializes outside the extraction root (write primitive). Falsifier: extraction rejects or canonicalizes entries (all entries land inside the extraction root), which disproves the weakness.
