evidence: Class prior: zip-slip is a durable MFT/extraction bug class; world model notes Apache Airflow lineage in MFT history (automation unpack flows). No archive endpoints mapped yet; passive GET of /robots.txt returned empty, /.well-known/security.txt timed out (no endpoint evidence either way).
falsifier: Disproven if every entry of a test archive extracts strictly within the extraction root (traversal sequences rejected, flattened, or canonicalized before write).

title: Path traversal in download/preview endpoint via filename or path parameter
detail: Secure file-sharing apps expose download and preview URLs; where the server resolves a user-influenced filename/path parameter to a filesystem path without canonicalization, '../' sequences escape the intended directory. INPUT: the filename or path query/body parameter on a download or preview endpoint (not the share-link token, to avoid the program-excluded 'anyone after authentication' authorization class). Confirming behavior: a traversal payload returns content from outside the intended directory tree. Falsifier: the endpoint resolves opaque IDs/tokens rather than paths, or canonicalizes and enforces a prefix check, yielding identical 4xx responses for traversal vs garbage input.
evidence: World model open question 3 (upload/share flow mapping in progress); no download endpoints mapped yet. Class prior: preview generators and download handlers are classic traversal sites in file platforms.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) download/preview URLs carry only opaque tokens/IDs with no path parameter; or (b) traversal and random-garbage inputs return identical error responses with no content differential across repeated trials.

title: Traversal via unsanitized original filename in bulk-download/export archive generation
detail: Kiteworks MFT supports bulk download/export flows that generate a ZIP server-side from user-selected files; if the server builds archive entry names from user-controlled original filenames, a filename containing '../' or '/' poisons the generated archive (self-inflicted archive poisoning: server later re-extracting or a recipient extracting writes outside the target dir). INPUT: the original filename supplied at upload time, later consumed by the export/archive-generation flow. Confirming behavior: the generated archive preserves traversal-bearing entry names verbatim. Falsifier: filenames are sanitized (slashes/dots stripped or replaced) before upload persistence, or archive entry names are generated from opaque IDs so the original filename never reaches the archive.
evidence: Class prior: export-as-ZIP flows in sharing platforms historically preserve raw filenames; world model confirms MFT is in scope with undetected stack. No upload or export endpoints mapped yet.
falsifier: Disproven if uploaded filenames with path separators are visibly normalized on upload (renamed/sanitized in the UI or API response), or if generated archives use opaque entry names rather than original filenames.

title: Traversal in preview/thumbnail cache write path derived from document path or name
detail: Document preview pipelines render files to a cache directory; where the cache filename is derived from a user-influenced document path or display name without canonicalization, '../' in the name can direct the cache write outside the cache root (write primitive) or cause cache-key collisions serving another file's preview. INPUT: document name or folder path feeding the preview renderer. Confirming behavior: a traversal-bearing document name produces a cache artifact outside the expected cache directory, or previews of distinct documents collide/swap. Falsifier: cache keys are content hashes or opaque IDs with no path derivation, or name-based keys are canonicalized and prefix-checked before write.
evidence: Class prior: preview/thumbnail caches are a recurring traversal site in file platforms; Kiteworks Core centers on file sharing with previews (open question 3). No preview endpoints mapped yet; passive surface check (robots.txt empty, security.txt timeout) gave no endpoint evidence.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) preview artifacts are keyed by opaque content hash or document ID; or (b) traversal-bearing names yield preview outputs identical in placement to sanitized names, with no file materializing outside the cache root.

title: BOLA-1: Comment endpoints bypass parent-file permission checks
detail: GET /rest/comments/{id}, PUT /rest/comments/{id}, DELETE /rest/comments/{id} operate directly on the comment ID. The API has file-scoped comment listing (GET /rest/files/{id}/comments) that implies permission is checked at the file level, but the bare /rest/comments/{id} endpoints may validate only authentication + that the comment exists, not that the caller has access to the parent file/folder. A comment ID harvested from a shared file could be read, edited, or deleted by a user with no access to that file.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restCommentsIdGet/Put/Delete on GET/PUT/DELETE /rest/comments/{id} as standalone operations; separate file-scoped listing exists at /rest/files/{id}/comments. No docs statement found tying {id}-level comment ops to parent-file ACL checks.
falsifier: Authenticated low-priv user requests GET /rest/comments/{comment_id} for a comment on a file they cannot access and receives 403/404 (or 200 only when the caller has access to the parent file).

title: BOLA-2: File member role update reachable by non-owner members
detail: PUT /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id} (Update members in the file) and DELETE /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id} (Delete member from the file) may enforce only that the caller is a member of the file, not that the caller holds owner/manage permission. If so, a read-only file member can elevate their own role to editor, or remove other members / the owner.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdMembersMemberUserIdPut/Delete on PUT/DELETE /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id}. Folder-level members endpoint POST /rest/folders/{id}/members (Add multiple members) exists as a separate bulk op. Docs do not state an owner-only requirement on the per-member update.
falsifier: A non-owner (viewer/editor) file member attempts PUT /rest/files/{id}/members/{other_user_id} to change a role, or their own role to editor, and the server returns 403 for every such attempt while owners succeed.

title: BOLA-3: Version promote action lacks per-object write check
detail: POST /rest/files/{id}/versions/{version_id}/actions/promote (promote specified file version) is a state-changing action on a version object nested under a file. It may check authentication and file existence but not the caller's write permission on the file, letting a read-only viewer rewrite file history (rollback attacks, content substitution behind a share link).
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdVersionsVersionIdActionsPromotePost on POST /rest/files/{id}/versions/{version_id}/actions/promote. Versioning endpoints include per-version content download (GET .../versions/{version_id}/content), so version objects are directly addressable by ID.
falsifier: A viewer-role member of the file (read-only, no write) attempts the promote action and receives 403, while an editor-role member succeeds.

title: BOLA-4: File content download keyed only on unauthenticated ID lookup
detail: GET /rest/files/{id}/content (Download a file) and GET /rest/files/{id} (Retrieve information about the file specified) take a bare file ID. If the ID-space is predictable/guessable and the authorization check is a single ACL lookup that fails open on shared-folder membership edges (e.g., caller has access to a PARENT folder but not the file, or was removed as member), a cross-user IDOR leaks metadata or bytes.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdContentGet (GET /rest/files/{id}/content) and restFilesIdGet (GET /rest/files/{id}). Program excludes 'anyone after authentication' file disclosure as an accepted-risk class, which signals the area is sensitive — hypothesis targets only access OUTSIDE the documented sharing model, not the excluded class.
falsifier: Requesting content/metadata for a file ID owned by another user (no shared relationship) returns 403/404 consistently, including for IDs adjacent in the ID space and for files whose parent folder was previously shared.

title: XXE via SAML IdP metadata XML import in admin authentication settings
detail: Entry point: admin console SSO/SAML configuration where the administrator imports or pastes the identity provider's metadata XML (standard Kiteworks admin flow for SAML 2.0 IdP integration). If the metadata XML is parsed server-side with a Java/.NET XML parser that resolves external DTD/entities (default-insecure DocumentBuilderFactory / XmlDocument settings), a crafted metadata file containing a DOCTYPE with an external entity could trigger XXE during import/validation. Confirming behavior: import response or validation error reflects resolved entity content, or an out-of-band request is issued to a collaborator URL embedded in the entity (blind XXE). Kiteworks product docs list SAML 2.0 IdP integration as a standard supported feature.
evidence: Public Kiteworks API/admin documentation describes SAML_2.0 as a supported authorization/authentication type (legacy Accellion admin guide mirrored at watoniworawi.weebly.com admin guide; Kiteworks data-form-security whitepaper lists 'OAuth 2.0 and SAML integration with enterprise identity providers'). Hunting-environment target unreachable from sandbox (curl timeout, browser.open no content), so no live confirmation of the admin SSO UI on the bounty host; passive grade only.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) IdP metadata is only consumed via copy-paste fields (entity ID, cert, endpoints) with no XML document parsing; (b) the metadata parser rejects DOCTYPE / disables external entities (disallow-doctype-decl or equivalent), so a benign probe DOCTYPE is rejected or ignored; or (c) metadata import is not exposed in the hunting environment.

title: XXE via Secure Data Forms / Web Forms definition import (XML templates)
detail: Entry point: Secure Data Forms (formerly Secure Web Forms) module lets admins design structured forms; if form definitions can be imported/exported as XML (common for form-builder products), the import endpoint parses administrator-supplied XML. A DOCTYPE with external entities in the form-definition XML could be resolved during import. Confirming behavior: entity content appears in the imported form's preview/fields, or a validation error echoes resolved content. Note: this is speculative on the format - Kiteworks docs describe web form design via admin guide/training video but do not publicly confirm an XML import path, so format must be verified first.
evidence: Kiteworks Statement of Work and best-practices docs describe Secure Web Forms as admin-designed predefined forms collecting structured data. No public doc found confirming XML-based form import; hunting host unreachable, so this rests on product-module existence only.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) form definitions are created only through the UI wizard and stored/transferred as JSON with no XML parsing; or (b) the import endpoint, if any, accepts only schema-validated XML with DOCTYPE rejected.

title: XXE via AS4/ebMS SOAP envelope parsing in MFT B2B transfer gateway
detail: Entry point: Kiteworks Managed File Transfer module handles B2B file exchange; enterprise MFT products commonly expose AS2/AS4 receive endpoints that parse SOAP/XML messaging envelopes (ebMS 3.0/AS4 uses SOAP with attachments). If the hunting environment exposes an AS4/SOAP receive endpoint, the eb:Messaging header/body XML could be parsed with external-entity resolution enabled. Confirming behavior: an external entity inside the SOAP body is resolved (reflected in the MDN/error or an outbound request), producing file disclosure or SSRF. Kiteworks public docs emphasize MFT as a core product; AS4/SOAP exposure on the bounty host is unverified.
evidence: Kiteworks MFT is a scoped product per the YesWeHack program page; AS4/SOAP endpoint existence is NOT publicly confirmed for Kiteworks (inference from MFT product category only). Hunting host unreachable; zero endpoint evidence.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) no SOAP/AS2/AS4 receive endpoint is exposed on the hunting environment; or (b) any such endpoint rejects DOCTYPE or uses a hardened parser (no external entity resolution observed on probe).

title: XXE in document preview/conversion pipeline via OOXML or PDF/XFA uploads
detail: Entry point: Kiteworks secure file sharing includes document preview/thumbnail generation; preview pipelines often shell out to converters (e.g., LibreOffice, Apache Tika-style text extraction). A crafted .docx (document.xml with external entities - rarely resolved by ZIP-based parsers, so lower value) or a PDF containing an XFA form (XFA is XML and has a documented 2025/2026 XXE history: CVE-2025-54988 / CVE-2025-66516 in Apache Tika XFA handling, disclosed via crafted PDFs) processed by the preview/extraction chain could trigger XXE. Confirming behavior: extracted/preview text contains resolved external-entity content, or an outbound request fires during processing. This is the highest-severity shape (authenticated-user upload -> server-side parse) but depends entirely on the converter stack, which is unmapped.
evidence: Preview/thumbnail conversion is standard in file-sharing products; the Tika XFA XXE (CVE-2025-54988, PoC published ~Sep 2026 per GitHub kmkz/exploits) demonstrates this exact class is live in 2026-era stacks. No evidence the Kiteworks hunting env uses a vulnerable converter; converter stack is unmapped on the bounty host.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the hunting environment performs no server-side document text extraction/preview (client-side rendering only); or (b) the converter chain is identified and rejects or sandboxes XFA/embedded-XML processing (e.g., XFA disabled in the parser config).

title: desanitize() decode-then-render: stored DOM-XSS via tenant config values
detail: /login_config defines desanitize(str) which HTML-entity-decodes server-injected config values ('->', &->&, "->", <-><, >->>) and strips ALL backslashes, applied to vue_config fields (serviceName, labels, disclaimer, ipBlockMsg, link.getStarted, link.contactUs, info.contactUs). If the Vue SPA renders any of these fields through an HTML sink (v-html/dangerouslySetInnerHTML/innerHTML) in the 21 unfetched chunks, a tenant/admin-set value stored HTML-encoded at rest is decoded back to raw markup client-side before injection = stored DOM-XSS affecting all tenant visitors. Not self-XSS (victim is other users of the tenant).
evidence: GET /login_config (200, 1190 bytes, 2026-09-27): full desanitize() source captured; signin.f7b86212.js chunk (49KB) contains zero innerHTML/document.write/eval sinks, so sink must be confirmed in remaining ~21 chunks. CSP is script-src 'self', which would block inline script execution but not necessarily non-script HTML injection impact.
falsifier: Grep the remaining /static/js/*.js chunks for innerHTML|v-html|dangerouslySetInnerHTML consuming vue_config/*config* fields; if all rendering is textContent/React-escaped with no HTML sink reachable from config values, reject.

title: Tenant-configurable link URLs rendered as anchor href with target=_new (javascript: URL)
detail: vue_config.link.getStarted, link.contactUs, info.contactUs are rendered as links with target=_new per code comment ('this part describe values used for links - a href target new'). Empty in this environment but tenant-configurable. If the app sets the href from config without scheme allow-listing, a tenant admin (or a tenant-config injection flaw) setting javascript:alert(document.domain) yields stored XSS executed in the victim's session on the login page. Source=tenant config, sink=anchor href assignment/navigation.
evidence: /login_config source: link:{getStarted:'',contactUs:''}, info:{contactUs:''} plus comment 'used for links - a href target new'. No scheme validation visible in /login_config or signin.f7b86212.js.
falsifier: Inspect link-rendering code in remaining chunks for href scheme validation (http/https allow-list) or confirm these config fields are not tenant-editable; if either holds, reject.

title: location.search query params flow into window.location.assign via x.fI URL builder
detail: In signin chunk: query params parsed from window.location.search by x.JO, merged into a URL by x.fI, then window.location.assign() executes it. If x.fI concatenates an attacker-controlled param value into the URL without scheme validation, a crafted link could navigate the victim to a javascript: URL (DOM-XSS) or external origin (open redirect). Source=location.search, sink=location.assign.
evidence: Code: z=e=>{...const s=(0,x.JO)(window.location.search);return(0,x.fI)(a,(0,y.A)((0,y.A)({},s),t))} followed by window.location.assign(...). CSP script-src 'self' would block javascript: navigation in modern browsers, reducing impact to open-redirect at most.
falsifier: De-minify x.fI/x.JO in the signin chunk; if x.fI enforces http(s) scheme or only merges into a fixed same-origin template, reject the XSS variant (open-redirect variant may survive separately).

title: Reflected username query param pre-fills login input via React state
detail: new URL(window.location.href).searchParams.get('username') is passed directly to a React state setter Y(s) that pre-fills the username field. If that value reaches any HTML sink (error messages, tooltips, aria labels rendered via innerHTML in other chunks), a crafted link gives reflected DOM-XSS. In the signin chunk the value only feeds React-controlled input state (auto-escaped), so the hypothesis depends on a sink in the remaining chunks.
evidence: Code: const s=new URL(window.location.href).searchParams.get('username');s&&(Y(s),r(f)). No innerHTML/document.write/eval in signin.f7b86212.js; CSP script-src 'self' present.
falsifier: Trace Y (the state setter) through remaining chunks; if the username value is only ever rendered via React text interpolation / input value props with no innerHTML path, reject.

title: SAML attribute→LDAP attribute role-mapping conflict grants inconsistent privilege sets across web UI vs mobile/API
detail: Identity integrations (LDAP/AD and SAML SSO) both drive role/profile assignment: LDAP uses attribute-driven role mapping (Bind DN, Base DN) while SAML IdPs (Entra ID, ADFS, Ping) supply assertion attributes that Kiteworks maps to roles. If a user exists in both the directory-backed path and the SAML path — e.g., an account first provisioned via LDAP then federated via SAML, or dual-auth enabled per-user — the two attribute mappings may resolve to different role sets and the resolution order (last-write vs merge) may differ between the web UI's session evaluation and the mobile/desktop API token evaluation. One code path could grant the higher-privilege role (e.g., Admin role attribute from LDAP) while the other grants the SAML-mapped lesser role, or vice versa: a downgrade in one surface and an escalation in another. This is a cross-feature interaction bug because each integration is tested in isolation against its own mapping config.
evidence: World model agent #14: LDAP/AD uses attribute-driven role/profile assignment; SAML 2.0 SSO (SimpleSAMLphp-style ACS) with Entra ID/ADFS/Ping drives both auth AND role assignment. Program focus explicitly lists privilege/role escalation.
falsifier: Create/provision (with program permission) one test account via both paths with intentionally divergent role attributes; inspect role evaluation in web UI session vs mobile/API token session. If both surfaces agree on one consistent role set, reject.

title: MIP sensitivity label consumed by EPG policy but ignored in share-link/DLP forwarding path enables label-stripped exfiltration of protected documents
detail: The Email Protection Gateway consumes Microsoft MIP sensitivity labels and RMS as inputs to policy rules (quarantine/encrypt/forward decisions). Separately, the file sharing path (share links, connectors like SharePoint/OneDrive/Box) downloads and forwards files via content connectors that preserve or re-apply remote ACLs but may not propagate MIP labels or RMS protection state to the DLP/ICAP verdict path, which is delegated to third-party ICAP servers keyed on file content. A document received via EPG that is correctly quarantined/encrypted at the email gateway could be re-shared through the web UI share-link feature or a connector sync (e.g., Google Drive/Box sync) without the MIP label or RMS protection intact, bypassing the label-based policy that protected it in transit. The security assumption broken: 'a document EPG marks as sensitive stays protected downstream.' Program-excluded 'AV bypass by file rename' does not apply; this is label-fidelity across feature boundaries, not file-type evasion.
evidence: World model agent #14: EPG consumes Microsoft MIP sensitivity labels and RMS in policy rules; connectors include SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, Dropbox; DLP verdicts delegated to external ICAP. EPG and connector paths were documented by different integration documents.
falsifier: Pass a test MIP-labeled document through EPG into a test mailbox, then share the same document via share-link/connector in the hunting environment and inspect whether MIP label/RMS state survives and whether ICAP/DLP verdicts match the EPG decision. If the label and protection survive with consistent verdicts, reject.

title: WithSecure Atlant scan-verdict timing vs ICAP DLP verdict mismatch lets a file that AV cleared but DLP would block be shared via the path that checks only one
detail: Embedded AV (WithSecure Atlant, on-appliance) and DLP/ATP/CDR (delegated to third-party ICAP servers: Forcepoint, Digital Guardian, Check Point SandBlast, Trellix) make separate verdict decisions at possibly different stages: AV on upload, ICAP DLP on share/send. If the share-link or email-gateway release path checks the cached AV verdict (file is 'clean') but does not synchronously re-check the ICAP DLP verdict — or vice versa: one path blocks on AV quarantined state while another path only awaits ICAP — a file can be in a transient or terminal state where one security verdict has not been enforced in the other feature's path. E.g., a file flagged by DLP as containing restricted data (not malware) passes AV and gets shared via the mobile app or Outlook plugin before or without the ICAP verdict, because the plugin path was built against the AV-scan state model. The trust delegation is split: block/quarantine/forward decisions depend on external ICAP verdicts, but each client path may subscribe to only one verdict source.
evidence: World model agent #14: AV is embedded WithSecure Atlant; DLP/ATP/CDR delegated to third-party ICAP servers; block/quarantine/forward decisions depend on external ICAP verdicts; clients include Outlook/Office plugins, mobile apps, desktop clients.
falsifier: Upload a test file that triggers a DLP rule (non-malicious, e.g., synthetic PII pattern approved by program scope) and no AV signature; attempt to share it through web UI, mobile-equivalent API path, and Outlook plugin equivalent; record whether any path permits sharing while the ICAP verdict is pending or after it fired. If all paths consistently enforce the DLP verdict, reject.

title: Share revocation does not invalidate in-flight download sessions
detail: State sequence: LINK_ACTIVE -> DOWNLOAD_STARTED (recipient begins chunked or ranged download) -> LINK_REVOKED (sender/admin revokes the share or disables the link) -> TRANSFER_CONTINUES. Hypothesis: access authorization is evaluated only at link resolution / first byte, and the download session (chunk tokens, range stream) is not bound to the share's live state. Confirming behavior: after revocation, subsequent chunk/range requests for the same transfer still return 200 and the full file is retrievable. This is a deterministic state-transition gap (revoke handler fails to purge active transfer sessions), not a timing race. Evidence: Kiteworks secure-share model centers on link states (active/expired/revoked) and per-file encrypted storage, but no public doc describes session invalidation on revoke.
falsifier: Revoke a share mid-download; if every subsequent chunk/range request returns 403/401 and the transfer terminates, the hypothesis is false.
evidence: none provided

title: Chunked upload session survives folder role demotion
detail: State sequence: ROLE=CONTRIBUTOR with UPLOAD_INITIATED (via POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload) -> ROLE_DEMOTED_TO_VIEWER (admin changes folder role mid-upload) -> CHUNKS_COMMITTED + FINALIZE. Hypothesis: the upload session capability is captured at initiation and chunk-commit/finalize handlers do not re-evaluate the caller's current folder role. Confirming behavior: after demotion, committing remaining chunks and finalizing succeeds and the file (or new version) lands in the folder. This is a deterministic check-missing-at-transition flaw. Evidence: public Kiteworks API docs describe initiateUpload/chunk/finalize mechanics and role-based folder permissions as separate concepts, with no stated re-authorization at finalize.
falsifier: Demote the uploader to viewer mid-session; if chunk commit or finalize returns 403 and no file materializes, the hypothesis is false.
evidence: none provided

title: Approval action on a withdrawn or expired transfer applies to stale state
detail: State sequence: TRANSFER_PENDING_APPROVAL -> SENDER_WITHDRAWS (or transfer expires) -> APPROVER_APPROVES via stale approval token/link. Hypothesis: the approval endpoint validates the approval token but not the transfer's current lifecycle state, so a late approval either returns a false success or resurrects the transfer into APPROVED/DELIVERED. Confirming behavior: approving a withdrawn transfer yields HTTP 200 success, or the transfer re-enters an active state visible to sender/recipient. This is testable sequentially (no race). Evidence: Kiteworks MFT/approval workflows are a documented product surface with pending/approved/denied states; no public doc describes approval-idempotency or state guards on withdrawn transfers.
falsifier: Approve a withdrawn/expired transfer; if the endpoint returns an explicit invalid-state error and the transfer remains withdrawn with no delivery, the hypothesis is false.
evidence: none provided

title: localhost:9999 MCP OAuth callback assumes one person per machine — shared-host code interception
detail: Assumption: the Kiteworks MCP Server OAuth flow's localhost:9999 callback is reachable only by the user who initiated it (one user = one person per machine). Violation: on multi-user hosts (terminal servers, shared jump boxes, CI runners, RDS sessions) the loopback interface is a shared namespace — a second local user can pre-bind or race-bind port 9999 (or sniff the redirect on a host without loopback binding protection) and capture the authorization code before the legitimate MCP client reads it. The code is then exchanged for an OAuth session bound to the victim's Kiteworks identity, because the callback has no per-user isolation (no SO_REUSEPORT guard, no secret state bound to a per-user channel, or state not validated). Confirming behavior: a test OAuth initiation from user A while user B holds port 9999 results in user B receiving the code and obtaining a token for user A's session. This is novel because the trust boundary (local machine = single principal) is an implicit OS-level assumption, not a documented Kiteworks feature.
evidence: World model agent #14: Kiteworks MCP Server (9.5+, OAuth app, localhost:9999 callback) for AI clients incl. Claude Desktop/Code. OAuth loopback-callback interception is a known class (RFC 8252) but whether Kiteworks MCP defends it (random port, PKCE, state binding) is unverified.
falsifier: On a shared test host, bind localhost:9999 as a second local user during a test MCP OAuth flow; if the flow uses an ephemeral random port, requires PKCE with per-session verifier, or refuses when the port is already held, reject.

title: Revoked API/OAuth tokens remain valid because resource servers validate signatures without a revocation check
detail: Assumption: revoking a token (OAuth app disconnect, admin session kill, remote wipe of a mobile/desktop client) immediately and globally ends that token's authority — 'revocation is global and immediate.' Violation: if API/resource-server validation is signature-and-expiry-only (JWT verified locally with no deny-list or introspection lookup), a token that was revoked in the identity store continues to authorize API calls until its natural expiry. Confirming behavior: after revoking a test token (or triggering remote wipe of a test mobile session), the same token still returns 200 on authenticated API endpoints minutes/hours later. Novel angle: the assumption breaks across the client fleet — desktop clients with long-lived refresh/session tokens and the MCP OAuth app are the high-value carriers, since their tokens persist outside the web session lifecycle. Note: program excludes rate-limit findings; this is authorization state, not rate limiting.
evidence: World model agent #14: desktop/mobile clients use OAuth sessions with remote wipe; Kiteworks MCP Server is an OAuth app; tokens are a documented surface. No public doc describes token introspection or revocation propagation semantics.
falsifier: Revoke a test OAuth/API token (via UI or remote wipe of a test client), then call an authenticated API endpoint with it; if every call returns 401/403 immediately after revocation, reject.

title: Case-sensitive username uniqueness vs case-insensitive mail routing yields two accounts sharing one mailbox
detail: Assumption: one email address maps to exactly one account (email = identity), and uniqueness checks enforce it. Violation: if the application enforces email uniqueness case-sensitively (or without Unicode normalization) while SMTP delivery and the corporate mail server treat local-parts case-insensitively, an attacker can register Admin@victim-domain (or a Unicode-normalization variant) as a distinct second account while all mail — including password-reset tokens — for both accounts lands in the same inbox owned by the original user... or worse, the second registrant claims a mailbox alias that the directory already routes to someone else. Confirming behavior: registering a case-variant of an existing test account's email succeeds in creating a second account, and a password-reset request for the original account's address is deliverable by/visible to the second account's owner (or vice versa). Novel angle: the identity assumption breaks at the seam between the app's string comparison and the mail infrastructure's routing rules — neither layer is wrong alone. This is distinct from program-excluded user enumeration (no probing for account existence; single controlled registration of own variant).
evidence: World model: authentication flows include LDAP/SAML/email-OTP; program focus includes privilege/role escalation and LDAP injection — identity-string handling is in focus. Email-uniqueness comparison semantics are unverified in the hunting environment.
falsifier: Attempt to register a case-variant (or plus-addressed variant, if the directory strips plus tags) of an already-registered test email; if the application rejects it as a duplicate account, reject.

title: Expired/download-exhausted secure link still serving via alternate retrieval path
detail: Kiteworks secure share links carry business rules: max download count, max view count, and expiration date (publicly documented; vendor guide also states files are deleted from the server after link expiry). Hypothesis: expiry/budget enforcement lives in the share-page controller, while a parallel retrieval path (direct download API, file preview/thumbnail endpoint, or secure-email attachment link) resolves the link token through code that checks only token validity. Rule combination: (link token valid) AND (expiry elapsed OR download budget exhausted) should uniformly deny, but if paths diverge, an 'expired' link still yields file bytes via the weaker path.
evidence: Public Kiteworks docs: links let users 'control access by restricting the number of downloads and views, and setting an expiration date'; Getting Started Guide: 'After the link expires, the files are deleted from the server.' No observed behavior yet - hypothesis only.
falsifier: Create a share link with max-downloads=1 and ~1-minute expiry using owned accounts. After 1 download or after expiry, request the file through EVERY retrieval path (share page, direct download URL, preview/thumbnail, API download). Hypothesis is FALSE if all paths uniformly deny (403/expired state) and the file is unrecoverable via any path.

title: Approval-chain step-skipping in MFT/forms workflow (out-of-order approval)
detail: Kiteworks MFT and Secure Data Forms support multi-step approval workflows: policy decisions include 'require additional approval' and audit logs record approver identities. Business rule: an item must be approved in order by each designated approver before release. Hypothesis: the approval-action endpoint validates 'actor is an approver on this workflow' rather than 'actor is the approver of the CURRENT pending step', so an approver assigned to a later step - or a submitter who also holds an approver role on the workflow - can approve out of order and collapse the chain, releasing a transfer that was supposed to require two-level (or N-level) review.
evidence: Kiteworks MFT compliance docs describe 'Approval workflows and approver identities' and policy decisions of permit/deny/require-additional-approval. No observed behavior yet - hypothesis only.
falsifier: With owned accounts, configure a workflow item requiring approver A then approver B. Have B (or the submitter holding an approver role) approve while step A is pending. Hypothesis is FALSE if the server rejects the out-of-order approval (403/422), the item stays blocked, and the audit log records the rejected attempt rather than a release.

title: External-recipient restriction enforced on share-link path but not secure-email path
detail: Kiteworks lets admins enforce domain whitelist/blacklist and external-sharing restrictions per profile (documented for SFTP and email policies: 'control user access, expiration, domain whitelist/blacklist'; secure email supports 'policies for expiration, forwarding, viewing, download access, and domains'). Business rule: user profile forbids sharing with external domains. Hypothesis: the share-link creation path and the secure-email compose/send path enforce this rule at different checkpoints, so a user blocked from creating an external share link can deliver the identical file externally by attaching it to a Kiteworks secure email - two code paths implementing the same business rule inconsistently.
evidence: Vendor docs confirm both paths exist with domain/profile policy controls: share links with granular access control; secure email with policy-controlled sending. No observed behavior yet - hypothesis only.
falsifier: With owned accounts under a profile that blocks external share links, attempt (a) creating an external share link - expect block - and (b) sending the same file as a secure-email attachment to the same external address. Hypothesis is FALSE if both paths consult the same domain/profile policy and both reject (or the email path is equal-or-stricter).

detail: Secure file-sharing platforms split access decisions across time: a share link is minted when DLP/policy allows it, but policies are re-evaluated later (file reclassified to a stricter label, sender's role changed, sharing-policy tightened). If the link's capability token is checked against only the issuance-time policy context rather than re-evaluating policy on each access, the link becomes a dormant bypass: it keeps serving content after the platform itself would deny it. This is not an 'auth bug' or a race condition — it is a temporal policy-evaluation desync unique to capability-URL + reclassifiable-content architectures. Confirming behavior: share a file under its current policy, then reclassify the file (e.g. apply a stricter sensitivity label) or demote the sharer, then re-access via the original unmodified link — 200 with content vs expected 403 is the signal. Distinguish from caching: the wrong behavior must persist after cache TTL and across nodes. Falsifier: if policy is verifiably re-evaluated server-side on every link access (e.g. access is denied immediately after reclassification), this class does not exist here.
evidence: World model: Kiteworks consumes Microsoft MIP sensitivity labels in EPG policy rules; program bounty focus includes privilege/role escalation; share-link flows are an open question (agent research pending). Policy-at-issue-time is the common design; per-access re-evaluation must be verified.
falsifier: A shared link issued before reclassification is denied (403) immediately after the file is reclassified to a stricter label or the sharer loses rights, with the denial persisting across cache expiry.
title: Dormant share-capability desync (policy re-evaluation skipped on share-link access)

detail: Governance platforms keep versioned files where each version is a separately addressable object, but the UI and API present only the 'current' version. If deletion/reversion of a version removes the version pointer while leaving the underlying object bytes addressable (e.g. via version-id parameters, version-specific URLs, or connector-proxied paths), an adversary with prior knowledge of the old version address can still fetch content the platform believes was destroyed. This is not broken access control in the generic sense — it is object-lifecycle incompleteness in version-addressed storage, a class with no standard name. Confirming behavior: upload v1 with sensitive content, upload v2 sanitized, invoke the platform's delete/revert on v1, then request v1's exact prior address/API path — content served instead of 404/410 confirms it. Falsifier: version deletion physically purges or cryptographically shreds the underlying object so prior addresses return 404/410.
evidence: World model: versioning semantics are an open research question for the hunting environment; Kiteworks MFT/ Core are file-centric products where version histories are standard. No evidence yet of how deletion is implemented.
falsifier: After deleting a file version through the platform's supported flow, its exact prior address consistently returns 404/410 (no content) after any propagation delay.
title: Version-slot desync (deleted file version remains addressable)

detail: Kiteworks delegates security verdicts to external ICAP servers (Forcepoint, Digital Guardian, Check Point SandBlast, Trellix) and audit/compliance is a headline feature. If the audit log records the connector-reported outcome ('blocked', 'scanned clean') rather than independently re-deriving the outcome from the data-plane result (what was actually served/delivered), then a misbehaving, unreachable-during-scan, or spoofed ICAP responder can create a divergence: the log says 'blocked' while the file was delivered, or vice versa. In a compliance platform the audit trail IS the product, so tampering-via-delegation is a novel trust class: evidence forgery through a delegated verdict pipeline. Confirming behavior: trigger a file flow through an ICAP-evaluated path and compare the audit-log entry against the actual delivered content/side effects — a mismatch (log says blocked, file arrived; log says clean, file quarantined) is the signal. Program exclusions do not cover this: it is not AV bypass by rename and not rate-limiting. Falsifier: audit events are generated server-side from the actual data-plane outcome, so the log and the delivered result never diverge.
evidence: World model (agent #14): DLP/ATP/CDR delegated to third-party ICAP servers; AV is WithSecure Atlant on-appliance. Trust boundary explicitly noted: 'file block/quarantine/forward decisions depend on external ICAP verdicts'. Audit-log integrity is an open question.
falsifier: Induced ICAP flows always produce audit entries matching the actual data-plane outcome (delivery/quarantine/block), even when the ICAP responder is slow, erroring, or returns conflicting verdicts.
title: Delegated-evidence divergence (audit trail derived from untrusted ICAP verdict)
Versioned content replacement inherits prior ICAP DLP/AV verdict
detail: Features combined: file versioning + DLP/AV delegated to external ICAP servers (Forcepoint/Digital Guardian/Check Point/Trellix per agent #14). DLP/AV verdicts in content-aware gateways are commonly cached per file object to avoid re-scanning every download; versioning creates a new content object under the same file identity. Emergent behavior: uploading a new VERSION of an already-scanned-clean file may skip the fresh ICAP verdict request and inherit the prior version's clean verdict, so policy-violating content introduced via version replacement is never re-scanned. Each feature is secure alone (ICAP scans new uploads; versioning preserves history) — the vulnerability exists only in the composition.
evidence: Passive docs only: agent #14 confirmed DLP/AV verdict delegation to third-party ICAP; versioning is a core Kiteworks file-management feature. No direct testing performed (analysis only).
falsifier: Vendor docs or audit events show a fresh ICAP verdict request is issued for every new version (a per-version scan/audit entry), or version replacement is implemented as delete+new-upload through the same scan path.

title: Share-link authorization snapshot survives LDAP role revocation (TOCTOU)
detail: Features combined: secure share links + LDAP/AD attribute-driven role assignment + DLP policy rules. Share links are created against a recipient's then-current directory attributes; LDAP group changes (role downgrade, DLP-policy reassignment, deprovisioning) happen asynchronously in the directory. Emergent behavior: a share link created while the recipient held an elevated or DLP-exempt role may continue to authorize access after the directory revokes that role, if the share's authorization was snapshotted at creation time rather than re-evaluated per access. Each feature is secure alone (shares are permissioned; LDAP roles update correctly) — the flaw exists only where the two interact, giving a window of unauthorized access to sensitive shared content.
evidence: Passive docs only: agent #14 confirmed LDAP/AD drives both auth AND role/profile assignment; sharing is a core feature. No direct testing performed (analysis only).
falsifier: Per-access re-evaluation of the share against live directory attributes (docs describe dynamic authorization, or an observed share stops working immediately after a role change), or share links store no role-derived permission beyond recipient identity.

title: MCP localhost OAuth callback interception feeds AI Data Gateway RAG
detail: Features combined: Kiteworks MCP Server (9.5+, OAuth app with localhost:9999 callback) + desktop/Outlook clients + AI Data Gateway for RAG. The MCP server enables AI clients (Claude Desktop/Code) to query Kiteworks content over OAuth. Emergent behavior: a malicious local process or a web page able to reach the localhost:9999 OAuth callback can intercept the authorization code during the MCP app flow; if the flow lacks strict PKCE + state + exact-redirect validation, the attacker redeems it for an MCP session token and then uses the AI Data Gateway RAG interface to query and exfiltrate the file content the victim can access. Each feature is secure alone (OAuth, desktop sync, RAG each have their own controls) — the vulnerability exists only in the composition of localhost-callback OAuth with a content-querying AI agent.
evidence: Passive docs only: agent #14 noted Kiteworks MCP Server (9.5+) with localhost:9999 callback and AI Data Gateway for RAG; desktop clients use OAuth sessions. No direct testing performed (analysis only).
falsifier: MCP OAuth flow enforces PKCE with strict state binding and exact redirect URI validation so an intercepted code is not redeemable by another client, or the MCP app scope excludes RAG/content-query capabilities.

title: EPG trusts MTA-supplied 'internal' markers, letting forged internal mail bypass gateway policy
detail: Trust boundary: app(Kiteworks EPG) <-> upstream mail server (customer MTA / M365 / any SMTP server). The EPG consumes mail from the customer's mail infrastructure and applies policy (quarantine/encrypt/forward, S/MIME, MIP-label rules). At this boundary the gateway must classify each message as internal (already authenticated by the trusted MTA) or external (full policy treatment). The receiving side's assumption: the sending MTA performed SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation and the message arrived over the trusted connector path, so MTA-added markers (Received chain, Authentication-Results, or X-headers used to signal 'internal') can be trusted for policy decisions. If classification relies on those headers rather than the gateway independently re-verifying DKIM/SPF, an attacker who can reach the gateway's SMTP listener directly from an arbitrary IP can forge the markers and have spoofed 'internal' mail skip encryption/quarantine. The broken assumption: 'headers describing authentication came from an authenticated source.' This is distinct from generic spoofing reports: the vuln is the gateway delegating its own authentication decision to unverified header claims.
evidence: World model agent #14: EPG works with M365/any mail server over SMTP; consumes Microsoft MIP labels and RMS in policy rules; SMTP-TLS/DMARC/DKIM listed as supported (not confirmed as gateway-enforced). Hunting env confirms /.well-known/security.txt and /robots.txt exist but the mail-receiving path of the appliance is not yet characterized.
falsifier: In a controlled test with program permission, deliver two otherwise-identical spoofed messages to the gateway SMTP listener: one with forged 'internal' markers (Received/Authentication-Results/X-headers) and one without. If both receive identical policy treatment, or the gateway rejects direct non-connector delivery outright, reject.

title: App trusts its LDAP filter construction; injected filter logic returns multiple entries and the app binds as the first match
detail: Trust boundary: app <-> LDAP/AD directory. Kiteworks binds with a service Bind DN, searches the Base DN with a filter built from the login username, then binds as the returned entry's DN with the supplied password. The receiving side's (app's) assumption: the directory returns exactly the entry the user identified, because the filter it constructed is interpreted as written. LDAP injection is explicitly a program focus area. If the username is concatenated into the filter without escaping, input such as `*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*` turns the search into a match-all; the app then takes the first entry (often alphabetically first, potentially a privileged account) and binds with the attacker's password. Even when the bind fails, differential responses between 'no entry found' and 'entry found, wrong password' become an oracle for directory structure and valid usernames. The broken assumption: 'the directory interpreted my filter as a single-user lookup.' The novel angle vs generic 'LDAP injection exists': the specific failure mode is multi-entry return + first-match selection, not just filter syntax error.
evidence: World model agent #14: LDAP/AD integration confirmed with Base DN, Bind DN, and attribute-driven role/profile assignment; program focus explicitly lists LDAP injection and privilege/role escalation. Multi-entry handling behavior is untested.
falsifier: With a test account and program permission, submit filter-metacharacter usernames to the login flow. If every malformed input is rejected or escaped into a literal-match lookup returning exactly zero/one entries with identical error handling, reject.

title: API trusts the client to be the enrolled device; OAuth refresh tokens lack device binding, so remote wipe is advisory only
detail: Trust boundary: mobile/desktop client <-> Kiteworks API. Clients (iOS/Android/desktop, OAuth sessions) advertise remote wipe and encrypted sync folders as controls. The receiving side's (API's) assumption: presenting a valid refresh/access token proves the request comes from the enrolled, compliant device — token possession is treated as device identity. If refresh tokens are plain bearer tokens with no DPoP-style sender binding or device attestation, a token exfiltrated from a lost device (backup, rooted device, desktop credential store) can be replayed from any client to pull synced folders, and remote wipe fails silently because wipe only works if the compromised client still checks in — the attacker simply never checks in. The broken assumption: 'the token holder is the wiped device.' Confirming behavior would be continued API access via replayed token after a wipe command is issued from the admin console.
evidence: World model agent #14: clients use OAuth sessions; remote wipe and encrypted sync folders are documented client controls. No evidence that tokens are bound to device keys; wipe depends on client cooperation by design.
falsifier: In a controlled test, issue a remote wipe for a test device, then replay its refresh token from a second client fingerprint. If the API rejects the token post-wipe (server-side revocation tied to the wipe command), reject.

title: Trusted-domain credential harvesting via Secure Data Forms
detail: A low-privilege authenticated user (or any user able to publish a form) uses Advanced Forms — a legitimate feature — to build a public form on the trusted Kiteworks domain mimicking IT/HR/security (e.g. 'Password reset verification', 'VPN re-auth'), with form-submission email notifications routed to an attacker-controlled address. Victims submit credentials/PII trusting the corporate domain; the attack never touches email, so phishing filters and DMARC/DKIM checks are bypassed entirely. Abuse-of-feature: no code bug required, only intended form publishing + notification routing.
evidence: World model: Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms in scope; EPG consumes M365 labels and applies mail policies, but forms live outside the mail flow. No evidence forms carry external-form warnings or restrict notification recipients.
falsifier: Forms cannot be published to anonymous/public submitters, notification emails are locked to the form owner's verified domain, or the platform marks externally-shared forms with an unremovable warning.

title: MCP Server turns AI client into a DLP-bypassing exfiltration channel
detail: The Kiteworks MCP Server (9.5+, OAuth app with localhost:9999 callback) lets a legitimate user connect an AI client (Claude Desktop/Code) with broad file-access scope. File contents then flow into the LLM's context window, where a malicious prompt, compromised skill/plugin, or simple 'summarize and send' instruction exfiltrates data through the AI channel — bypassing the DLP/ATP/CDR ICAP policies that only inspect Kiteworks-native transfers. The insider's access is fully authorized; the exfiltration path simply isn't a 'transfer' the policy engine sees. Abuse-of-feature: intended AI integration, unintended egress channel.
evidence: World model: MCP Server and AI Data Gateway for RAG exist in 9.5+; security verdicts (DLP/ATP/CDR) are delegated to external ICAP servers that evaluate file transfers, not LLM context consumption. No evidence DLP policies apply to MCP-mediated reads.
falsifier: MCP tool scope requires per-file/per-folder user consent, DLP/ICAP policies are evaluated on MCP-mediated file reads, or the MCP server is admin-gated and off by default in the hunting environment.

title: Stored connector credentials as a lateral-movement bridge
detail: Enterprise Connect / content connectors (SharePoint, SMB/CIFS/DFS, Documentum, Google Drive, Box, Salesforce, iManage) store backend credentials so Kiteworks can sync behind-customer-firewall content. A user holding connector-admin rights — but NOT domain/backend admin — abuses this legitimate feature to pivot into connected backends using the stored credentials, reaching file shares and repositories their own identity could never touch directly. The trust boundary is the credential vault: if stored creds are usable beyond narrowly-scoped sync actions, connector administration becomes de-facto backend administration.
evidence: World model: connectors listed with note 'Trust: stored connector credentials and remote-ACL fidelity' — flagged as a key trust boundary. LDAP/AD drives role assignment, so a connector admin may be a low-privilege directory user.
falsifier: Stored connector credentials are vaulted and never exposed to any user session, sync actions are executed under a least-privilege service identity with remote-ACL enforcement, and connector administration is restricted to the same role that already owns the backend.

title: Self-edit attribute + profile mapping rule = auto-promotion (H-PRCHAIN-1)
detail: Chain: (1) a low-privilege user changes a self-editable profile attribute (e.g. department/title/email-alias) via update_user; (2) an admin-defined profile mapping rule auto-assigns a privileged user profile by matching that attribute (agent #20: rules match by username/email, testable via get_profile_eligibility). Each step alone looks benign — editing your own profile is expected, and mapping rules matching is by design — but the chain turns a self-service edit into privilege escalation: the account gains feature privileges (profile layer) without any admin performing assign_user_profile. Combined impact: privilege/role escalation (program bounty focus).
evidence: Agent #20: three-layer privilege model (users start with ZERO privileges until a profile is assigned), profile mapping rules auto-assign by username/email match, update_user mass assignment candidate (H4).
falsifier: Profile mapping rules are only evaluated at login/SSO-sync time and never re-evaluated after self-edit attribute changes, or update_user does not permit changing rule-matched attributes — confirm by changing a matched attribute and observing the profile stays unchanged across a fresh session.

title: LDAP/SSO JIT attribute + missing admin-strip = first-login elevation (H-PRCHAIN-2)
detail: Chain: (1) LDAP/AD attribute-driven role/profile assignment or SAML assertion attributes feed JIT provisioning (agent #14: directory/IdP drives BOTH auth and role assignment); (2) documented guard — create_user strips admin roles — may not be enforced on the SSO JIT/LDAP sync path (agent #20 H6 unverified). An account whose directory attributes claim a privileged group would land with elevated profile/role at first login while the interactive create_user path blocks the same outcome. Each step alone is low-impact (attribute sync is by design; JIT provisioning is by design), but the chain yields privilege escalation at account birth with no admin action. Combined impact: privilege/role escalation (program bounty focus).
evidence: Agent #14: LDAP Base/Bind DN + attribute-driven role assignment, SAML SimpleSAMLphp ACS; Agent #20: create_user strips admin roles (unverified on JIT/LDAP paths).
falsifier: JIT/sync path demonstrably applies the same strip — provision with an admin-claiming attribute and the account lands with default/zero privileges, same as the create_user path.

title: Forged MIP sensitivity label + ICAP-delegated verdict = EPG policy bypass (H-EGCHAIN-3)
detail: Chain: (1) Email Protection Gateway policy rules consume Microsoft MIP sensitivity labels and RMS (agent #14); (2) actual AV/DLP block/quarantine/forward decisions are delegated to third-party ICAP servers (Forcepoint, Digital Guardian, Check Point SandBlast, Trellix). If a label can be forged or downgraded before policy evaluation (label integrity depends on RMS validation by the gateway, not the ICAP server), the chain lowers the DLP/ATP verdict: a sensitive file exits via email that a correctly-labeled file would not. Each step alone is low-impact (label mis-set is cosmetic; ICAP verdicts work as configured), but combined they defeat the data-protection control. Combined impact: DLP policy bypass leading to unauthorized sensitive-data egress via email.
evidence: Agent #14: EPG consumes Microsoft MIP sensitivity labels and RMS in policy rules; AV is WithSecure Atlant on-appliance while DLP/ATP/CDR verdicts are delegated to external ICAP servers.
falsifier: The gateway cryptographically validates MIP/RMS labels before policy evaluation and rejects or quarantines files with forged/downgraded labels — confirm by submitting a file with a manipulated label and observing it does NOT receive a lower-sensitivity verdict.

title: Link-expiry data destruction guarantee contradicted by retained derived copies
detail: Docs CLAIM: the Getting Started Guide states 'After the link expires, the files are deleted from the server.' Observed/plausible REALITY: 'deleted' likely means the share link and primary file pointer are removed, while derived artifacts — preview/thumbnail renditions, full-text search index entries, ICAP DLP/AV verdict caches keyed on file hash, and AV-quarantine copies of the same bytes — remain server-side and potentially addressable. The divergence is a documented destruction guarantee vs a soft-delete implementation. Security relevance: users/share senders relying on the documented guarantee to destroy sensitive files (legal/compliance holds, PII purge) may be silently non-compliant; retained derived copies may also be reachable via alternate paths (preview endpoint, search API).
evidence: Getting Started Guide quote: 'After the link expires, the files are deleted from the server' (cited in agent #66 hypothesis). Agent #14: AV (WithSecure Atlant) and ICAP DLP/AV verdicts (Forcepoint, Digital Guardian, Check Point SandBlast, Trellix) inherently cache verdicts per file/hash; file previews/thumbnails are standard for a file-centric platform. No public doc describes deletion scope across derived stores.
falsifier: After an owned share link expires, verify byte-level absence of the file in primary storage AND derived stores (no thumbnail/preview retrievable, no cached ICAP verdict re-served for a re-uploaded identical file, quarantine purge confirmed). If all derived copies are demonstrably destroyed, reject.

title: Documented zero-privilege user start vs default-profile fallback on automated provisioning
detail: Docs CLAIM (agent #20, REST/admin docs): the privilege model is three-layer and 'users start with ZERO privileges until a profile is assigned' — least-privilege-by-default. Observed/plausible REALITY: the zero-privilege invariant was documented for the interactive user-creation path; automated provisioning paths (SSO JIT provisioning, LDAP/AD sync) commonly fall back to a default profile or a system-generated profile when no profile-mapping rule matches, and that default profile may carry folder access, share rights, or app permissions the admin never assigned. The divergence is between the documented universal invariant and a provisioning path that never evaluates it. Security relevance: silently over-privileged accounts for every SSO/LDAP-provisioned user — a privilege/role-escalation adjacent configuration vuln (program focus area), especially where profile-mapping rules are misconfigured.
evidence: Agent #20 docs-grade: users start with ZERO privileges until a profile is assigned; profile mapping rules auto-assign by username/email match. No evidence the strip/zero-start invariant holds on the SSO JIT or LDAP sync paths, which bypass create_user. World model open question #2: auth flows and roles unverified in the hunting environment.
falsifier: Provision test users through SSO JIT and LDAP sync with no matching profile-mapping rule; if each lands with literally zero privileges (no folder access, no share capability) exactly as documented, reject.

title: create_user admin-strip guard bypassed by SSO JIT and LDAP sync provisioning paths
detail: Docs CLAIM (agent #20, /adminRoles REST API docs): the create_user REST endpoint ignores/strips any admin role on input, and 'only system admins can promote users to application admins' — a documented enforcement invariant against self-promotion. Observed/plausible REALITY: the strip is implemented in one endpoint's input validation, but SSO JIT provisioning and LDAP/AD sync are separate code paths that construct user records directly from directory/assertion attributes (attribute-driven role assignment). If those paths do not re-apply the strip, a SAML assertion carrying an admin-role attribute or an LDAP entry with a privileged mapped attribute promotes the user without any system-admin action — the documented invariant holds only on the path it was documented for. This is distinct from generic 'mass assignment': the divergence is the spec claiming a platform-wide guard that is actually endpoint-local. Security relevance: direct path to unauthorized admin role (program focus: privilege/role escalation), exploitable where the attacker controls IdP/LDAP attribute values.
evidence: Agent #20 docs-grade: create_user strips admin role (enforcement on other paths explicitly marked 'unverified'); 'only system admins can promote users to application admins' per adminRoles docs; LDAP attribute-driven role/profile assignment and SAML SSO both drive role assignment per agent #14. No evidence JIT/LDAP paths enforce the same strip.
falsifier: Demonstrate (in docs or with owned test accounts and program permission) that SSO JIT provisioning and LDAP sync apply the identical admin-role strip: provisioning a user with a privileged mapped attribute yields a non-admin account in all three paths. If all paths strip uniformly, reject.

title: Legacy HMAC-SHA1 'Signature Authentication Method' still mints API tokens
detail: Old Kiteworks/Accellion admin guides document a legacy OAuth token flow: build base_string = client_id|@@|user_id|@@|timestamp|@@|nonce, sign it with HMAC-SHA1 using the app signature key, and POST an auth_code of the form base64(client_id)|@|base64(user_id)|@@|timestamp|@|nonce|@@|sig to the token endpoint with an X-Accellion-Version header. Because the API still documents/accepts X-Accellion-Version (an Accellion-era brand header), this legacy auth-code path may still be validated server-side on the hunting environment alongside modern OAuth.
evidence: Mirrored Kiteworks admin guide shows the full HMAC-SHA1 signature auth-code flow including header X-Accellion-Version: '8' and scope strings like */admin/*; SEC's published Kiteworks user guide (sec.gov kiteworksguide_0.pdf) confirms Accellion-era flow lineage. Accellion->Kiteworks rebrand was late 2021 with explicit backward-compat migration support for customers.
falsifier: A correctly-formed legacy signature auth-code request to the token endpoint is rejected as an unknown/unsupported grant or method (e.g. unsupported_grant_type or a message naming the signature method as removed), rather than failing only on invalid client credentials - showing the code path is gone, not just our credentials.

title: 123FormBuilder-era legacy form endpoints live inside Secure Data Forms
detail: Kiteworks acquired 123FormBuilder and rebranded it as Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms (in scope). Acquired products are typically wrapped rather than rewritten: legacy 123FormBuilder URL patterns, public form-submit endpoints, legacy webhook callbacks, or legacy signing/version parameters may still resolve on the hunting environment behind the new UI, with older, less-hardened validation than the modern Advanced Forms paths.
evidence: Program scope explicitly lists Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms; public record shows 123FormBuilder was acquired and folded into Kiteworks. 2026 CVEs in Secure Data Forms (CVE-2026-24755 stored XSS, CVE-2026-24756/24761/24782 IDOR classes) are consistent with an older form-engine code base still in service.
falsifier: All form-related URLs on the environment resolve only to the modern Advanced Forms paths; legacy 123FormBuilder-style URL patterns and webhook endpoints return 404 or redirect without serving form functionality - showing no legacy form engine is exposed.

title: Accellion-era version-compat shims (X-Accellion-Version) still change server behavior
detail: Legacy client code sends header X-Accellion-Version: '8' and the API historically negotiated behavior by Accellion version number. If the server still parses that header for backward compatibility with migrated Accellion customers, requesting an old version value could activate older response schemas, deprecated fields, or code branches that no longer receive security fixes - a classic forgotten-feature surface.
evidence: Official-era code sample in the mirrored admin guide sets X-Accellion-Version: '8' on token requests; Accellion EOL'd FTA in April 2021 and provided migration assistance to Kiteworks, which historically kept version-negotiation code paths alive server-side.
falsifier: Varying X-Accellion-Version (e.g. '6', '7', '8') produces byte-identical responses compared to requests without the header, and legacy versioned API paths return uniform 404s - showing the version shim is parsed-but-ignored or fully removed.

title: Delegated admin roles can alter or purge audit events, defeating the platform's governance claim
detail: Kiteworks sells auditability as its core value. Nobody asks who can edit or delete the audit trail itself. Expected control: audit events are append-only/tamper-evident; retention and purge settings are system-admin-only with retention locks; delegated roles (helpdesk, application admin) have read-only access. Its absence matters because a rogue or compromised delegated admin could exfiltrate governed data and then erase the download/access evidence, removing the very record the product promises customers.
evidence: World model: delegated admin roles with configurable component scope; agent #14 notes trust boundaries everywhere except the audit store; no documented immutability or retention-lock control found in docs-grade material
falsifier: Audit events are immutable in storage, delegated admin roles have no delete/edit/purge path via UI or REST API, and retention-policy changes require system admin plus a retention lock.

title: DLP/ATP ICAP delegation fails open when the ICAP server is unreachable or errors
detail: AV/DLP/ATP/CDR verdicts are delegated to third-party ICAP servers (agent #14). Expected control: the appliance fails closed — quarantine or block uploads/downloads — when the ICAP server is unreachable, times out, or returns an error. Its absence matters because the entire upload/share flow (the product's core) would then pass malicious or DLP-violating content with a governance stamp of approval whenever the external verdict service degrades, which is exactly the moment attackers would target. Agent #68 covered verdict timing mismatch; nobody asked about availability-failure behavior.
evidence: Agent #14: file block/quarantine/forward decisions depend on external ICAP verdicts; no documented fail-closed behavior found in docs-grade material
falsifier: The appliance demonstrably quarantines or blocks (never permits) file operations while the ICAP endpoint is unreachable or returns an error, and this behavior is not configurable to fail-open by non-system admins.

title: Delegated admins can reset credentials or 2FA of system admins, enabling top-down account takeover
detail: The three-layer privilege model and delegated admin roles are mapped (agent #20), and everyone studies promotion paths upward. Nobody asks the reverse: who can perform credential lifecycle actions (password reset, 2FA enrollment/disable) on privileged accounts, including system admins. Expected control: credential/2FA resets on admin accounts are system-admin-only with dual authorization or out-of-band verification, so a delegated admin cannot lock out or take over the admins above them. Its absence matters because a single compromised delegated-admin account could cascade to full appliance control by resetting the system admin's credentials and disabling their 2FA.
evidence: Agent #20: 8 default + custom delegated admin roles with configurable component scope; credential-lifecycle scoping for admin accounts not addressed in docs-grade material
falsifier: Password resets and 2FA changes on any admin account require system-admin scope with dual authorization (or equivalent out-of-band check), and delegated roles cannot target accounts at or above their own privilege level.
